speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: From the banks?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
From the banks here, or
in the United States or in Great Britain. My hon. friend will realize, though it is difficult to realize now, the exceedingly critical condition that prevailed immediately following the outbreak of the war. This was in September. The moratory legislation in England prevented our banks as well as outside banks from obtaining payment, even had they desired it, of deposits which they had with institutions in Great Britain. In this connection I may point out that in many cases companies, Arms, and, I suppose, individuals in Canada, who had provided for credits in advance in order to meet maturing liabilities in Great Britain, found themselves in the position, by reason of the moratorium, of not being able to avail themselves of credits so established.
As I said, both railway companies were earnestly requested by the Government to obtain loans from Canadian banks, or in the United States or in Great Britain, but they were unable to do so. Both the Prime Minister and myself took the opportunity to

consult with the bankers of the railways concerned to ascertain that the statements made by the railway companies in this respect were correct. In the circumstances two alternatives presented themselves. The first was to allow the railway companies to shut dowm construction work and disband their organizations. This would have involved the dismissal of about twelve thousand men engaged in the construction work of both companies. It would have meant the loss to the contractors of their organizations. It would have meant also that the supply businesses engaged in furnishing material and provisions to these organizations would suffer heavy loss and the trade of the country would be seriously inconvenienced thereby. By reason of the fact that interest would continue to run against the companies, it would have meant also that the Government's own security under these mortgages and under former legislation with regard, to both systems would be diminished and the date of their completion indefinitely postponed. The disbandment of existing organizations, of course, would have meant increased expense in assembling them at a later date for the purpose of completing construction. The other alternative was that the Government should make advances directly to the two companies upon their securities bearing its guarantee to ensure completion of their systems-that is, to effectuate the intention of Parliament in giving the guarantee. In giving the matter consideration it was borne in mind that Parliament, at the August session, had granted to the Government powers of a very far-reaching character under the War Measures Act of 1914, section 6 of which is as follows:
The Governor in Council shall have power to do and authorize such acts and things and to - make from time to time such orders and regulations as he may hy reason of the existence of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection, deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada.
That would extend to company railway matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was coming to that a little later on, but may deal with it now. The Minister of Justice, I think, would be prepared to give his opinion-though it is not relevant, because I stated when the subject was referred to earlier in the session, that I did not propose to rely upon the War Measures Act-that if the Government considered the issue of these securities to be lMr. W.. T. White.]
of public interest during the period of the war it would be open to the Government to make such issues. But, as I have stated, I do not intend to rely upon that. I refer to it only for this reason-to show that an exceptional condition existed and was -recognized by Parliament in August last. For the War Measures Act would obviously not have been enacted under normal conditions. The powers conferred by that Act would not have been conferred under normal conditions, but only as stated in the Act, "In case of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection.'' The object of that legislation was to empower the Government to take such action in the public interest as the exigencies of the war might require and which, in normal times, could and should only be taken by the consent of Parliament.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there was no power in the Government to make advances from Consolidated Revenue Fund, upon the security of these guaranteed bonds and debenture stock. The only possible method that was open to the Government to assist in the completion of this enterprise which . the Government regarded as desirable in the public interest was to make advances in Dominion notes. There wtfs no other means to accomplish the end, namely, the completion of these lines, than the issue of Dominion notes by way of advances. As the banks were unwilling to intervene as borrowers from the Government on behalf of the companies, it became necessary, if the situation was to be met, that the Government should make the advances directly to the railway companies themselves upon the securities in question. Advances were accordingly made of Dominion notes from month to month upon the guaranteed securities at the rate of 80. The agreement of pledge taken from the railway companies was the same as that which has been taken from the banks in connection with advances made to them under the authority of the Finance Act of 1914. I may say that no question arises so far as the security is concerned. It is only a short time ago that Canadian Northern railway securities, guaranteed by the Dominion, were sold at a net price of 91J. As I stated, although I believe, the Minister of Justice would have been prepared to advise the Government that it had authority to make these issues-

What authority?
I do not understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Section 6 of the War Measures Act.
That is, the Minister of Justice would advise that the advance should be made out of the $50,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not necessarily.

It is not very important, but it does seem strange to me that such a contention as that put forward by the Minister of Finance should be made, and I cannot understand how it could be sustained. Of course, I do not say it is important.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Except that this exceptional legislation did exist. This legislation has no necessary relation to the war vote of $50,000,000.

In considering the interpretation of a statute, I think the minister should keep strictly within the rule that a statute should be interpreted in the light of the history of its time, the circumstances under which it was enacted and what was in the minds of the legislators when it was passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend. I do not propose to rely upon this statute; if I did, I should not be asking for confirmatory legislation. I believe the action of the Government is within the War Measures Act, but, as I was about to say, as we had specially amended the Dominion Notes Act in the August session and as we had in addition enacted the Finance Act of 1914, both relating to issues of Dominion notes, it appeared to me, as stated in the Order in Council, that the issue made by executive authority should be validated and confirmed by Parliament.
That seems to be right.
When the minister is trying to get on solid ground by means of new legislation, I do not think he will help his case by propping it up upon an untenable interpretation of the War Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Under the Dominion Notes Act, when notes are issued they go into the Consolidated Fund Account. The result of the net issue under the Act of August last gave the consolidated fund account $15,000,000, and there would be $10,000,000 under the other issue.. Did this $25,000,000 actually go into the Consolidated Fund account, and does it appear in the

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: calculations of the Minister of Finance of his total revenue for the present fiscal year, namely, $120,000,000? If not, why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not included in the $120,000,000. The $120,000,000 is the revenue of the Dominion; an issue of Dominion notes constituted a liability on the part of the Dominion. It is true that the Dominion used the $15,000,000 to which my hon. friend has referred, and the $10,000,000, or a total of $25,000,000, but it is just as if they had obtained a bank credit for that amount.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Just the same as if you had borrowed it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You add them to the public debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All added to the public
debt. Any increase of Dominion notes expands the public debt. But if, on the other hand, you hold gold against the Dominion

notes, your net debt is not increased, because the gold is a set-off.
With regard to the $10,000,000 issued for the general purposes of the Dominion, I may say that we have now $1,200,000 of gold against it, and it will be the policy of the Government gradually to redeem that $10,000,000, as has been done in other countries-as is being done in Great Britain today.
My attention has been called to certain newspaper .articles in which it has been said that these resolutions ask Parliament practically for a blank cheque for the issue of Dominion notes. The committee will observe that the resolutions are confined solely to the confirmation of the issues of Dominion notes aggregating $26,000,000 to which I have referred. The reason why a wrong impression got abroad was that it appeared to the Government last fall that, having regard to the critical condition which prevailed in all international markets, it might be necessary, and indeed that it would be necessary, for the Dominion Government to increase the Dominion note issue; and therefore in one of the Orders in Council, I think in the November one, it is stated that it was the intention of the Government to apply to Parliament for legislation which would authorize an increase in the Dominion note issue, secured by only 25 per cent in gold, to $80,000,000 instead of $50,000,000, as was done at the August session, or such other .amount as the exigencies of the war might require. I am glad to say that there has been such a wonderful improvement financially throughout the world -in London, in New York and in Canada- that it will not be necessary for the Government to consider the question of further extending the Dominion note issue or to ask for any legislation giving them that authority. As I stated, the policy of the Government will be to gradually redeem the $10,000,000 of Dominion notes issued for these general purposes; and, as the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern Railway securities which we hold are sold, to redeem the notes issued against them. If that programme is carried out, as I think it will be, we shall have our Dominion note issue in accordance with the express provisions of the Finance Act, 1914.
Will that be by redemption or by building up your reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Either way. For example, if we acquired gold and added it to our gold holdings, then the issue to that extent would be quite regularized under the Dominion

Notes Act. I omitted to say that the advances which we made in Dominion notes to the two railway companies
12 m. were deposited to the credit of ' the Receiver General to be paid out under the terms of the trust mortgages securing the issues in accordance with the Acts authorizing the guarantees. For the further information of the committee, I may say that, at the end of December last, the proportion of gold to Dominion notes outstanding and not otherwise secured was 65.82 per cent; at the end of January, it was 65.83 per cent; at the end of February, it was 65.88 per cent. These percentages are higher than the percentages prior to 1903, when the rate was 62 per cent. It may be interesting to the committee to know that, under the terms of the Federal Reserve Act of the United States, the federal reserve banks are required to maintain gold reserves equal to 40 per cent of their outstanding circulation. These notes are issued to the federal reserve banks by the Federal Reserve Board on receipt of collateral security consisting of notes and bills accepted for rediscount under the provisions of the Act. Under this advanced legislation a gold reserve of 40 per cent is considered sufficient, that is in the United States.
The action of the Government in making this advance is justified, we believe, so far as the $10,000,000 issue is concerned, on account of the necessity of maintaining the Dominion's credit in the emergency of the war, which made it impossible for the Government to borrow. So far as the advances to the railway companies are concerned, the justification is, in our view, the effectuation of the intention of Parliament that the two lines should be completed; the fact that the companies were unable to sell or borrow upon the guaranteed securities; the public necessity that the unemployment and the great loss that would result from the closing down of construction should be averted; and, lastly, the interest which the Dominion Government has as guarantor that its security should not be diminished by the loss of interest which would have resulted had construction been discontinued for an indefinite period. The statement I have made to the committee this morning shows the extent to which the Dominion has had to go in the issue of paper money not secured by gold.
The House may be interested to know how far other countries have been obliged to go since the outbreak of the war. The British Chancellor of tne Exchequer, in August last, undertook to issue paper currency and to deposit with banks asking for advances an amount equal to 20 per cent of their deposits and current liabilities.

Would the minister
state that again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Would that have been Bank of England notes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
We have legislation
enabling us to issue Dominion notes. Has England any legislation for the isue of what they call Bradburys?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Bradburys were first issued, I think, and then legislation ob-

tained validating what had been done and providing for the further issues which I have mentioned. I believe there is no limitation to the amount. In the United States the situation at the outbreak of war was similar to that which existed in Great Britain and ^anada, but fortunately the Aldrich-Vreeland Act had been amended in the previous year and, although up to that time it had not been availed of, it proved exceedingly useful in meeting the financial exigency of the war as experienced in the United States. Under that Act the banks were authorized to issue additional security, not exceeding $90,000,000, against cotton and tobacco secured notes, instead of as against United States bonds as previously, and under this measure the United States banks issued $363,000,000 of excess note circulation to meet the situation created by the war. In addition to that the Government deposited with the banks throughout the United States about $320,000,000, which, of course, was exceedingly helpful. I have taken probably an unnecessary amount of time in fully explaining these measures to the committee, but I realize that they are of great importance. Under normal conditions, in fact under even trying conditions, a Government, generally speaking, would not be authorized to take the action which this Government has taken in making these Dominion note issues. But by reason of the exceedingly critical situation created by the war and its effect upon international finance, which was described in my Budget speech of August last, and in the Budget speech of the present session, and is well known to all the members of the House, the Government felt justified in taking the executive action which I have described, feeling confident that their action would be subsequently confirmed by the House by reason of the exceptional circumstances which prevailed at the time the action was taken, and the objects we had in view in taking it. Having regard to the measures which were deemed essential, and which were taken in Great Britain, France and the United States, to say nothing of Germany, it must be conceded that on the whole Canada, a belligerent nation, has come through the crisis with as little amendment to her financial legislation and as little enlargement to her currency facilities as probablv any other nation.

Before the minister concludes I should like to say just a word. We have at the present time a Dominion note issue of $76,000,000, of which

$50,000,000 is authorized under the Dominion Notes Act of August, 1914, ail'd the rest of which is, to be legalized by the Bill to be founded on the resolutions we are now considering. Therefore we shall have two pieces of legislation authorizing this total note issue of $76,000,000. It struck me as the minister was speaking that it might have been better to amend in some form the Dominion Notes Act so that all the legislation on this subject would be contained in one Act, or in the principal Act and an amending Act. There is no guarantee, of course, that the Government will redeem the excess circulation of $26,000,000 within any specified time, or that they will build up an additional gold reserve of $26,000,000 against this excess note issue, so as to come within the requirements of the Dominion Notes Act. I do not say there is much importance in the point I am making, but I am interested in knowing whether the minister has considered it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have considered the point to which my hon. friend has drawn attention, and I have thought it better that the action of the Government should be confirmed by Parliament. I desire to leave the Dominion Notes Act precisely as it is, for I do not think it wise that we should enlarge the free Dominion note issue provided by that Act. Now it is true, as my hon. friend has pointed out, that there will be $26,000,000 of Dominion note issue legalized by the confirmation which Parliament will, we hope, now give to the action of the Government. But, as I have pointed out, it will be the policy of the Government to gradually reduce that amount, and according to my conception the $26,000,000 will be gradually redeemed; and the Dominion note issue will then stand as the original Government issue of Dominion notes. I think this was the course followed by the Government in 1908, when legislation was introduced confirming the action of the Government in making advances to the banks in 1907 during a critical financial period. Now, as soon as those loans were paid off, that confirmation was exhausted, and the Dominion Government then continued to be governed by the express provisions of the Dominion Notes Act. Once the notes that had been issued in excess of the amount authorized by the Dominion Notes Act were redeemed, there was no power by reason of the validating legislation for the Government to re-issue those notes.

As a matter of fact,
I do not think the loans were ever made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes.

As the Minister of
Finance has stated, this is very important legislation. Further, it is very intricate and technical, and I trust that anything I shall say will be accompanied with becoming modesty, and be taken as an endeavour to express my own views, rather than the opinion of any other hon. gentleman.
I think this is the first occasion in the history of Canada in which the authorized Dominion note issue has been exceeded, for reasons such as those now urged by the Minister of Finance. Our previous authorizations to extend the Dominion note issue were, if I recollect aright, due to two causes, the first of which was due to the expanding business of the country which necessitated an increase in the available paper money for our commercial needs, and the second occurred in 1907; the justification then being a currency stringency. I am not disposed to agree with the Minister of Finance that under the legislation passed last August there was authority for this excess note issue, but as he does not rely on that as a justification, and comes to Parliament asking for legislative confirmation, it is not necessary that I should deal with that phase of the question. There was no authority to make advances to the Canadian Northern Railway Company or to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company upon their own securities guaranteed by the Government of Canada, nor was there authority for the note issue made in respect of each of these two advances in Dominion notes. We, therefore, have two unauthorized acts on the part of the Government, and the question before us is a consideration of whether the circumstances were such as to justify these acts. I am not disposed to find very much fault with the action of the minister in making advances to the railway companies, because, no doubt, it was of great importance to the railway companies and to the country that they should be able to carry to completion their undertakings during the past year. These advances were made upon the authorized securities issued by the company and guaranteed by the Government of Canada. They were not, of course, liquid securities and could not be immediately realized upon, but inasmuch as they were guaranteed by the Dominion, one can hardly contend
that the security was not good. If the time ever comes when these are not a good security, then Canada and Canadians will be in a serious plight indeed. It is to be noted also that these securities were accepted at a discount of twenty per cent, which under the circumstances I would think a fair reduction to make. I am not disposed, therefore, to find any fault with the note issue made upon the securities of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I have not perused the Orders in Council very carefully, but I am assuming that these advances to the companies, upon their own securities, are for a fixed period, and that upon the termination of that period the country may look for a payment of the advances. If the financial conditions then are such that the railway companies cannot meet these obligations, there will no doubt be some arrangement by which the maturity of the advances may be extended on just terms.
The note issue of ten million dollars is in a somewhat different position from the note issues made to provide advances to the railway companies, and which the minister states the railway companies were unable to secure from the banks. Perhaps I should here say tha,t I am pleased that the minister is in a position to state that the Prime Minister and he urged upon the banks to make these advances to the two railway companies, under the Financial Measures Act of last year. I think it would have been preferable had the railway companies secured the desired advances in this way. It would have relieved the Government of the responsibility of making unauthorized issues of Dominion notes. I do think that in the circumstances the banks should have met the request of the Prime Minister and his Finance Minister, particularly as it meant no financial risk on their part, and they would immediately have received Dominion notes from the Government. Of course, it would have increased their liabilities which perhaps they desired to avoid.
I am glad to have the assurance of the Minister of Finance that he does not purpose allowing this entire excess note issue to remain outstanding indefinitely, He proposes either a redemption of the excess note issue, or its justification under the terms of the Dominion Notes Act by the increase of the gold reserve so that the issue will come within the provisions of that Act. That being the case,the situation is very different from what it would have

been, had the minister come to Parliament asking for authority to increase the note issue from $50,000,000 to $80,000,000, as was proposed in the Order in Council of November 2, 1914. On the whole, I am very glad that the minister has taken this view of the matter; that he is only seeking confirmation of the action he has taken, and that he has given the committee an assurance of his intention to redeem those notes or to meet the requirements of the Dominion Notes Act so far as gold reserve is concerned in respect to that issue. Our paper currency has always been regarded as being in an extremely safe and sound condition; and it would be unfortunate if, at any time or under any circumstances, we departed very far from the requirements of the Act. I trust this will only be done under the most compelling of necessities. I shall reserve any other remarks until we are considering the Bill to be founded upon these resolutions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Just a word to complete what has been said by my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). I take the same view as he does. I am very glad that the legislation goes no further than to confirm the issue of $26,000,000 of notes which was authorized by the Government last fall. At the August session we gave power to the Government to issue Dominion notes to the extent of $50,000,000 upon a gold basis of 25 per cent. The system upon which the credit of Canada rests is that every dollar issued out of the treasury in paper must be represented by gold in the treasury; but ever since that system was introduced, we have given a certain leeway to the Government, allowing a small proportion of Dominion notes to be issued in excess of the gold reserve. At the August session we increased that amount from $30,000,000 to $50,000,000; but the country was somewhat disturbed last fall when we heard that the Government intended to increase it from $50,000,000, to $80,000,000 upon the same gold reserve. The Government, however, does not intend to bring down legislation to confirm that intention. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, has just stated that the financial situation has so improved that he sees no necessity now to ask what he intended to ask, and that, he will limit the legislation to where we left it in the month of August last; that is to say, the Dominion will be authorized to issue paper currency to the extent of $50,000,000 and no more. The Government, however, has

made an extra issue of $26,000,000, and its intention now is simply to confirm that illegal act, so far as it was illegal, because it was against the law, and nothing more. The Government does not urge that its power to extend that issue be confirmed, so that when that $26,000,000 has been recouped to the treasury, the Government will not have power to issue another dollar upon the legislation which we are about to pass. Once this transaction is completed, there is no more to it. When the Government has been recouped for the advances which it has made to the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific and to the public at large, when those notes come back to the treasury, they are not to be reissued. The power of the Government is limited simply to the $50,000,000 and no more.
So far as Parliament is concerned, the only question before us today is whether or not the Government was wise or could be justified in issuing the $26,000,(500 which it issued, as stated by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in the very lucid explanation which he gave to the House th: ; morning. There has been some departure from sound principles. The basis of our legislation is that the credit of the country should not be used except under the strict terms of the law, but there are circumstances in which the Government is allowed to make some departure from the strict letter of the law. The late Government, over which I presided, did so in 1907. At that time the business of the country had so expanded that the ordinarv credit was found to be insufficient to move the crops of that, year. Upon finding that to be the case,, we thought we were justified in issuing Dominion notes to the banks so as to help the business of the country to go on. Our action was justified. In that case, however, we took for our issue absolutely liquid assets, and that is the object which the minister must have before him. He should make advances upon securities of that kind, so that if a sudden demand were to come to him, he could readily convert his assets into gold and meet his liabilities to the public. In this instance, 1 realize that my hon. friend could not secure liquid assets. The credit of the country was so disturbed by the war that he found it utterly impossible to obtain the liquid assets which he otherwise would have been expected to secure; but the securities which he obtained were of the best character that could be desired, because

they were securities, guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada. So far as that is concerned, no criticism can be offered against my hon. friend. The only criticism is that I think he should have taken that power last session, and he should be censured for not doing so. The correspondence shows that one of the companies, the Grand Trunk Pacific, came to him for assistance, and it would have been preferable if he had then taken the power which he is asking now. There would have been no difficulty in giving him that power, under the circumstances within the authority of Parliament, there can be only one excuse for the Government exceeding the authority of Parliament, that is, when there is a sudden demand which there was no possibility of for-seeing.
In this ease, my hon. friend should have foreseen that he would require that money, because the application had already been made. It was not a demand arising after the session of August, hut it had arisen before that session. But, so far as that goes, the point is not essential; the matter is one which we can overlook because, after all, " Salus populi suprema lex." In such circumstances as my hon. friend was confronted with, I agree with him, it would have been deplorable that the work of these two companies which is of such importance should not have gone on; and that it is better that he should have taken the action he did rather than have such a disturbance of business as would have occurred if these two companies had at once ceased their operations. On the whole, I have no hesitation in saying that we ratify the action taken by the Government, especially as we are now certain that the action is purely unique, that it is not general, but is confined to this one transaction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There are only one or two observations I desire to make. So far as taking express authority for this purpose at the last session is concerned, I may say to my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and to the House that we had no reason to apprehend at this time that these advances would not be made by the banks. The best security that could be given to any bank was available-the bonds of the railway companies guaranteed by the Government of Canada. We had many conferences with the hanks on the subject, and we thought, and still think, that it would have been better that the advances should have been made in that way. How-97
ever, the banks had their idea of the extent to which they should develop their liabilities on the one hand, and their assets on the other: they thought it would not be desirable or prudent for them to take the course which was suggested. Then, as was pointed out-and I need hardly repeat it- the two alternatives before the Government were either to have the organization of these railway construction companies broken up, thousands of men thrown out of employment, the business and economic conditions of the country disturbed, and the confidence in the future of the country greatly diminished; or, on the other hand, to take the course which was taken. After giving to it as careful consideration, I think, as has ever been given to any subject by the present Government, we concluded that we ought to take the course which was taken. I may say-though the question is only academic at the present moment-that I have not the slightest doubt that we had the power to take this action under, the War Measures Act of 1914 if we had seen fit to do so. I say that for the obvious reason that section 6 authorizes the Governor in Council to perform such acts as he, by reason of real or apprehended war, etc., deems necessary or advisable " for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada." Now, the general words under which this Parliament received power to legislate for Canada are that it may " make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada." The words which confer power on the Governor in Council are quite as wide, and I think we might have exercised that power under the War Measures Act. But I thought, and my colleagues thought, notwithstanding the belief that we could have done it in that way, that powers of that kind ought not to be exercised to the widest limit except for the gravest possible reasons. So we decided that if we were to take the course of advancing money upon the securities of these companies guaranteed by Canada, we had better not proceed under the War Measures Act, but pass an Order in Council which would distinctly state, as these Orders do state upon their face, that we were doing that with the intention of having our action afterwards submitted to Parliament, and ratified by Parliament if it should approve.
We took tnat course, and I am very glad to learn that it has met with very little criticism on tne other side of the House; because hon. gentlemen there as here,"



153d
realize that the conditions were urgent:	I
may say, looking back at the two or three months which succeeded the outbreak of the war that perhaps none of us to-day fully realize just how much public opinion in this country was oppressed by - the conditions which prevailed and how grave the situation seemed to us at that time. I for one can testify that the responsibility placed upon the members of the Government in connection with all these matters were of so grave and weighty a character that I most sincerely hope I shall never be called upon to pass through anything of the same kind again.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Now, with regard to the period for which the loan was made: I understand that it will expire very shortly [DOT]-at the end of this month. If renewal be necessary, as possibly it may be, it will be for only a fixed period. There was no idea of making the loan of an indefinite duration. And in order to reassure the House with regard to the situation, so far as the note reserve is concerned,.I may say that within two or three months after the first issue was "made we were assured by one of these railway companies, I think by both, that the securities given could be sold at an advance of from eight to ten points upon what the Government had advanced upon them.
If there had been any grave condition with regard to our currency, we could have consented that that should have been done; but it was believed by the Minister of Finance and by the companies themselves that with a little more delay the price that could be obtained would be greatly increased. Of course, the loss of three or four points upon the sale of any of these securities meant that just so much less money would be available for the purpose of carrying the construction of these roads to completion. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has been compelled to leave his place to keep an engagement, but if there is further information desired which, it is within my power to give, I shall be glad to give it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to say just one word to justify the criticism I have offered, that this legislation should have been sought during the August session. I quote from the Order in Council of the 5th September, 1914:

The committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 5th August, 1914, from the Minister of Finance, submitting the following facts:
(1) At the last session of Parliament an Act was passed known as " The Grand Trunk Pacific Guarantee Act, 1914," whereby the Government of Canada was authorized, for the purposes therein mentioned, to guarantee the payment of the interest and principal of an issue of bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for a principal amount not exceeding sixteen million dollars.
Then it goes on to say in section 4:
(4) By reason of the effect of the war upon financial conditions in Great Britain and elsewhere the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has been unable to sell or procure advances upon the said guaranteed securities either in London or in New York. The company' has also been unable owing to prevailing financial conditions, to obtain any loan from Canadian banks.
The minister therefore authorizes the issue of Dominion notes to the extent of $60,000,000. This was the report of the Minister of Finance to the Privy Council on August 5. Everything that is necessary should be done to maintain the high standing which Canada's credit has in the financial world, and it is essential to the maintenance of that high standing that the law should be strictly carried out. In my esti-.mation, the Government should in August last have taken the powers which they are now taking. There has been some fear on the part of the public that the Government might resort to the very unhealthy practice of issuing paper currency. We have the assurance of the Minister of Finance today, however, that there is no such intention that any idea which was entertained in the month of November of increasing the Dominion note issue from $50,000,000 to $80,000,000 will not be carried out. Whilst we ratify the action taken by the Government, I think it will be agreed that it would have been safer and more in accordance with the fitness of things and with tlie maintenance of the high standing of Canada's credit, if the provisions which we are now making had been made in the August session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I doubt very
much whether the date referred to is the correct date of the report. My right hon. friend will notice that the Order in Council was approved by His Royal Highness the Governor General on September 5. It may be that it came before us at that time;, I do not recollect it; but if it did come before us at that time, the view we had was that this ought to be done through the

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
financial institutions of the country, the banks. After the session of Parliament closed, the managers of two of the largest Canadian banks were asked to come to Ottawa, and it was urged upon them that any advances made by the Government ought to be made through the banks in the way which had been provided for by Parliament. I really saw at that time no great reason why it should not be done in that way, because, although the amounts were large, compared with the enormous business done by the largest banks in Canada, it would not seem an excessive amount for them to have undertaken, particularly as they would have been granting the loan upon the security of the Dominion of Canada. They were so doubtful about it, however, that we could not convince them that it was their duty to undertake it under the circumstances, although we sincerely hoped and believed that, upon reconsideration of the attitude which they had adopted at first, they would be willing to go that far. So we proceeded in the course to which my hon. friend has referred. 1 entirely agree that if we could have definitely foreseen that the banks would decline to take business of this kind, it would have been better to have brought the matter to Parliament at the last session and to have obtained authority in advance rather than after the transaction had been carried out by the Government. With my hon. friend's opinion in that regard I am in perfect agreement.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

speechtext:
motion of Hon. Frank Cochrane (Minister of Railways and Canals), the House went into committee, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair, to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to enact as follows :	'
1.	That it is expedient to provide that the Minister of Railways and Canals may, subejct to the authority of the Governor in Council, construct, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire, in whole or in part, any railway, railway bridge] railway station, railway terminal, railway ferry or other railway work in the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Is.and ; prov del that a copy of every such lease or contract shall be laid before Parliament ; and provided, further, that no railway so leased, purchased or otherwise acquired shall exceed two hundred miles in length; and provided. that no contract for the construction of a railway exceeding twenty-five miles in length shall be entered into until after a sum ot£f money for the purpose has been appropriated by Parliament; provided, further, that any such railway or other work when so constructed, leased or purchased, shall form part of the Government railway system; and provided that no such railway shall be so constructed, leased or otherwise acquired unless it directly connects with some part of the then existing Government railway system.
2.	That it is expedient to ratify and confirm an agreement dated the first day of August, 1914, between the Intercolonial Railway Company of New Brunswick, Thomas Malcolm, railway contractor, and His Majesty the King, for the sale to His Majesty of the railway and whole undertaking of the said company, extending from Campbellton, at the head of the Bay of Chaleurs, to St. Leonards, on the Saint John river, a distance of about one hundred and twelve miles, for the sum of two million seven hundred thousand dollars, payable any time within five years from the date of said agreement ; and to provide that, pending the payment of the purchase money, His Majesty may lease from the said company, for a period not exceeding five years from the date of said agreement, the said railway and undertaking at a rental of ninety thousand dollars per year, payable in equal half-yearly instalments, the first half-yearly payment of such rental to be made to the company on the first day of February, 1915 ; and to provide that the purchase money and rents payable by His Majesty may he paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
3.	That it is expedient to ratify and confirm an agreement dated the eighteenth day of March, 1915, between His Majesty the King

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
and the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island Railway Company, for the sale to His Majesty of the whole of the railways and undertaking of the said company, including the main line of the railway of the company extending from Sackville, in the province of New Brunswick to Cape Tormentine, in the said province, a distance of about thirty-six miles, for the sum of two hundred and seventy thousand dollars; and to provide that, until the purchase price is paid, His Majesty shall pay to the company interest on the said purchase price at the rate of 4 per cent per annum from the first day of August, 1914, the first payment of such interest to be made on the first day of August, 1915, and thereafter on the first day of August in each year; and to provide that the purchase money and the interest payable by His Majesty may be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
Mr. COCHRANE; This is simply a copy of the Bill that was introduced into this House two years ago. At that time the Senate unfortunately did not see eye to eye with this House. The second section of this resolution is to confirm an agreement for the purchase of the International railway, which starts from Campbellton and runs to St. Leonards, a distance of 112 miles. What has hurried on the purchase is the construction of the International bridge down there, which, but for this purchase, would have meant the taking away of a large amount of traffic from the Intercolonial. This line of railway will also be the means, I tjiink, of giving the shippers down there a cheaper rate to the New England States, and the Intercolonial will make nearly as much out of it as if it were carried around the other way. Physically the road is in very good shape, with the exception of one curve near Campbellton, and we hope to have an item in the estimates to provide for the straightening out of that part of the line. The third section of the resolution is to confirm the purchase of the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island railway, which we have bought with the object of connecting up the Intercolonial with the Prince Edward Island ferry. We are leasing the International railway for a certain number of years at a little less than 3i per cent on the purchase price, and have the option of purchase. As regards the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island railway we have to pay 4 per cent until the House passes the the legislation authorizing the purchase.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When this
resolution first appeared on the Order Paper, it was in the form of three separate 'resolutions. It is true that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister told me he want-

ed to present it as one resolution. As to that I have no observation to make, but no reason has been given to me why we should have only one resolution when three 'separate and distinct subjects are dealt with. 1 think it would have been preferable to have three separate resolutions. The second and third sections of this resolution apply to railways intended to serve the public in the Maritime Provinces, and to those no objection can be taken. The resolution to acquire the International railway is not objectionable from the point of view of the Intercolonial, for it will facilitate business between the province of New Brunswick and the Eastern States. That is a praiseworthy object, and to it we on this side of the House can have no objection, nor can we object to the third section, which provides for the lease or purchase *of the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island railway.
But the first one is of such a character that I hope to have a fuller explanation of .it than has been given by the minister. It is a resolution to buy railways here, there and everywhere.
The Minister of Railways has pointed out that in the session of 1913, this legislation passed the House of Commons, but that an amendment was made to it in the Senate, which the Government did not accept, but which, for my part, I think there was a good deal of merit in. We are entitled to know what the minister intends to do under this legislation. A resolution such as this, so broad in its terms, has not been brought before Parliament a second time without the Minister of Railways having given it a good deal of consideration. The hon. gentleman does not designate in the resolution any of the railways or works he intends to take over, although I presume he must have in his mind some scheme. This legislation is due to the efforts of our late colleague, Mr. Emmer-son, who session after session brought to the attention of the House the desirability of the Intercolonial Railway acquiring all the branch lines connected with it, and which are not now operated by that system. His view was, that these branch lines should be operated by the Intercolonial for the benefit both of the Intercolonial and of the public generally, and everybody will agree that there is considerable merit in that proposition. It is a notorious fact that these branch lines give very little satisfaction to the phone, that the companies which operate them have not the means of putting them in first-class

condition, and that if they were administered by the Intercolonial Railway they perhaps would not be unprofitable for the' railway, while they would certainly be of great benefit to the people. It was contended that even if it involved a loss to the Intercolonial railway the loss would be more than compensated by the great advantage which would enure to the public. These views were presented repeatedly to the House by my late colleague and friend, Mr. Emmerson, until at last they impressed the Government, and hence this legislation. We should know from the minister now whether action under this legislation is intended to be confined simply to the branch lines connecting with the Intercolonial. There are these qualifying words in the resolution :
Provided that no such railway shall be so constructed, leased or otherwise acquired unless it directly connects with some part of the then existing Government railway system.
The words "then existing Government railway system" are new words in the resolution, and they would seem to apply to any Government railway which does not exist to-day, but which may exist at any time in the future. The Minister of Railways would have power to acquire railways, bridges, stations, or any other works, not only this year but next year, or ten years hence, if the Act is not repealed in the meantime. The words "then existing Government railway system" seem to me to confer upon the minister a very wide power. We are entitled to know from the minister to what works and railways he intends to apply this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen will remember that during the election campaign of 1911, it was one of the planks of the Conservative platform that if the Conservatives came to power the Government would acquire the different branch lines along the Intercolonial, which it would be in the interests of the Intercolonial and of the country generally to acquire. A Bill was introduced in the session of 1911-12 in order to carry out that policy, but unfortunately it did not go through this House. It was again introduced in an amended form in the session of 1912-13, and passed this House, but was rejected in the Senate. The proposition is to acquire any railway covered by the resolution, any branch line along the Intercolonial railway or the Government railway, which it will be in the general public interest to acquire. At the present
time, the people living along these branch lines have to pay a double rate, the local rate and the through rate on the Intercolonial, and if these lines were acquired as part of the Intercolonial, the shippers would get the advantage of a through rate, which would be greatly beneficial to the community. It is a question whether some of the railways down there are worth very much, but I am not here to run down any branch line. I do not think the clause is so wide as my right hon. friend thinks, because its wording ties us down to branches connected with the Government railway system.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Intercolonial railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Any government railway. I cannot see what objection there would be to this resolution, even if we were to extend the Intercolonial and acquire branch lines, if it, were in the public interest to acquire them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I want to know where we are and what is intended. We all understand what the Intercolonial railway is, and we know that the government railways to-day are confined to the Intercolonial and the Prince Edward Island railway. Later on, it is quite possible there may be other government railways, and this resolution would then cover all these railways acquired by the Government. I do not object to it, but I want to know what we are doing. I understand that the object of the minister to-day is to acquire branch lines of the Intercolonial, and the reasons he has given satisfy me, and I hope they will satisfy the House, that such is desirable. The hon. gentleman tells us that at present there is double management and that there are double rates, and that it would be to the advantage of the people that there should be one management and a through rate, and so far I quite agree with him. I agree that he should be allowed to acquire these branch lines, which at the present time have been built at the expense of the people of New Brunswick, and which do not give to the people all the advantage they should derive from them. As I understand the intention of my hon. friend, it is to acquire thoise branch lines. So far, so good. I take that as the policy of the Government.
That point being settled, I come to another point, that which was at issue between this House and the other branch of this Legislature. The amendment to

this Bill came into this House two years ago in the dying hours of the 'session. We had a rather hot session and perhaps were not as well disposed or as equable in temper as we are at the present time; but now that our blood has had time to cool off and that we can approach the question, in perfect good temper, I will present to my hon. friend the views expressed in the other branch of the Legislature. I was not in the House when the Bill passed through this Chamber two years ago. When I came back, I took up the amendments made by the other Chamber, and I was told that the Bill as it left 'this House bad been agreed to by both sides. That is true, I believe. My hon. friend, however, will agree with me that -the two .sides of the House, even when they are unanimous, may not be absolutely perfect, and no one will contend that, when the two sides have agreed upon something, that it is the incarnation of wisdom and that it is impossible to make any improvement.
Two different powers are granted to the Minister of Railways under this Bill. First of all, 'he is empowered to acquire any existing railway, there being no limitation upon his power except that such railway shall not exceed in length 200 miles. If the railway exceeds 200 miles, he has no power to purchase it. Then he is given power to construct any railway that he deems advantageous in the interest of the country, provided it does not exceed in length 25 miles. If he constructs such a railway, he is hound to bring the matter	before Parliament; but his
power is limited to this, that the money	must	he voted	by Parliament. Parliament has complete control over his action if he constructs a railway twenty-five miles in length, but Parliament is not given power over his action if he buys a railway of two hundred miles in length. There is no reason why the same rule should not apply in the one case as in the other, that is, that the action of my hon. friend, acting as Minister of Railways or as the Government, should be submitted to Parliament for ratification. All that the amendment of the other branch of the legislature proposed was that, whether the contract was for the purchase of a railway existing already or for the construction of a railway by the minister, the money should be voted by Parliament. That amendment is not only legitimate, but the very essence of parliamentary government. My hon. friend will rather hesitate to take upon him-

self the power to buy a railway 200 miles long, dispensing with the authority of Parliament, when the mere fact of a signed contract binds Parliament to accept it. My hon. friend should allow his resolution to be so amended as to conserve over it the control of Parliament. If he were disposed to accept it, I would suggest an amendment to that end. I do not know whether or not it would cover the ground absolutely, but at all events it would meet the case in some way. I move the following amendment:
That there be inserted in line 2 of section 1, after the word " lease " the words " either with or without an agreement to purchase."
That is to say, the minister can lease, and he can put into the lease a clause empowering him to purchase. That amendment would make the clause read as follows:
That it is expedient to provide that the Minister of Railways and Canals may, subject to the authority of the Governor in Council, construct, purchase, lease, either with or without an agreement to purchase, or otherwise acquire-[DOT]
I think there can be no objection to that amendment.
I also move the following amendment:
That in line 9 of section 1, there be inserted, after the words " entered into," the words, " or the purchase price of any such railway or other work be paid."
The section would then read as follows:
And provided that no contract for the construction of a railway exceeding 25 miles in length shall be entered into, or the purchase price of any such railway or other work be paid, until after the sum of money for the purpose has been appropriated by Parliament.
I move these two amendments without asking my hon. friend the minister at the present time either to approve or to reject them. He will do well to take them into consideration. It is well to meet the criticism of the other legislature, which seems to me to have been in the right direction.

While the Prime Minister is considering the amendment, I may say that I saw in one of the Government papers to-day a statement to the effect that the Government proposes to operate the National Transcontinental railway sys-tetrn as part of the Intercolonial. We ought to have a statement in regard to that announcement, which is an important one, in connection with this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: If that is so, the point made by my right hon. friend is very important, because if my hon. friend proceeds to operate the National Transcontinental railway as part of the Government railway system, then there will be power given to him under this first section to take over branch lines which may extend all the way to Winnipeg. That would be a very wide power. Will the minister tell me what are the branch lines which he contemplates taking over this year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As far as the
first amendment proposed by the right hon. leader of the Opposition is concerned, there is no objection to it at all. So far as I understand the purport of the second amendment, it has this effect, that no contract for the construction of a railway exceeding 25 miles in length shall be entered into, or the purchase price of any such railway or other work be paid, until after the.sum of money for the purpose has been appropriated by Parliament. Perhaps that language might have been inserted so as to make the meaning clearer. As I understand it, the intention is that the Minister of Railways shall be given authority to pui chase a line of railway not exceeding 200 miles in length, but the price must not
, paid until the money has been appropriated therefor by Parliament. I do not suppose the money could really be paid until it has been voted by Parliament; therefore I really see no objection to what my hon. friend proposes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Under this legislation the Minister of Railways is empowered to make a contract. Of course, the money could not be paid unless voted by Parliament, but if Parliament gives to the minister the power to make an absolute contract, Parliament will be bound to vote the money later.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I quite understand my right hon. friend, and, if it is thought that this amendment will make the provision clearer, I have no objection to it. As to the other matter to which reference has been made, at the last session of Parliament the Minister of Railways and Canals was authorized by legislation then passed to operate any portion of the National Transcontinental railway at the completion
of the line, before the lease should be entered into. The difficulty-if there should be any difficulty, a discussion of which I shall not enter into at the present time-is this: that neither the statute nor the contract which provided for the construction of the National Transcontinental railway contains any definite method for quickly settling the question as to whether the joad at any time is so completed as to make it necessary that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company shall accept a lease. One would have expected to find in the statute some better method of determining that 'question than seems to be provided. In case any difficulty should arise, therefore-and I am not for a moment apprehending any difficulty-a delay might ensue over the period during which that particular question might be under consideration. That question would have to be determined in one of two ways: in the first place by agreement with the parties, or, in the second place, by the determination of some tribunal board of arbitrators, or court of law. If it should be necessary to resort to the second method-and I do not predict that it will be necessary-it is perfectly obvious that some delay would occur, and the Government would not like to have the road left in a situation which would prevent its being operated. That is to say, it is in the interest of the public, in the interest of the road itself, and in every conceivable interest, that there should be some operation during any necessary period for determining whether or not the road is completed to such an extent as to make it incumbent upon the company to accept a lease. It is purely that, I think, to which the Minister of Railways has reference. I should be perfectly willing to restrict this legislation so that it could have no possible application to any portion of the National Transcontinental railway which the Government might find it necessary to operate, because that is not in our mind at all. If any amendment is desired to that end, I shall be glad to consider it.
As to the power to take branch lines, it may be said that there are no branch lines on tne Transcontinental Railway at the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is one, I think.

If the Government were operating temporarily, wouiu the Transcontinental be a part of the Government

"system of railways? I hardly think it would, because I think that by statutory definition the Government system of railways consists of the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island railways.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think
this legislation would cover the case of temporary operation by the Government of the National Transcontinental railway. All the Government has in mind is not to leave the National Transcontinental railway unoperated if any question should arise which might cause delay.
Would it be a part of the Government railway system?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think so, but I am perfectly willing to have that made plain.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We understand, then, that this legislation applies to the Intercolonial only?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
And to the
Prince Edward Island railway. That is thoroughly understood.

Will the minister
say whether under this legislation he proposes to deal with the Vale railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I do not think it is in the public interest that I should make any announcement as to what railways I intend to deal with.
I understand, you have made arrangements?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Temporary arrangements were mads down there. The arrangement is not yet completed.
When are you going to tell us about it? .	..

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: When it is completed.

speechtext: Last evening, I asked the Minister of Militia and Defence for a statement of the cost of the upkeep of the militia who were in service in British Columbia since the outbreak of the war up to the present time, and the minister promised to have it to-day.

And I understand that that amount is chargeable to the war expenditure?
Major-General HUGHES: Yes.

Does that cover the total expenditure made by the minister in British Columbia for war expenses?
Major-General HUGHES: Yes, and a number of these men have since gone to the front.
Are there two thousand men on duty now in British Columbia?
Fully that Many. We have one regiment in Vancouver, and one regiment of cavalry, a regiment of infantry being organized, all for the front, and one in Westminster, a'=^ for the front.
I was not speaking of those volunteering for overseas service.
The only ones we have on home duty are the guards along the railway.
This expense of over a million dollars given by the minister is for militia on service in British Columbia.
Yes.
The memorandum will appear in Hansard, and I shall have great pleasure in bringing it before council.

I take this opportunity of again protesting against the very unfair action of the Government in refusing to extend the provisions of this Act to the province of Prince Edward Island. There are a number of men still living in that province who, at the time of the Fenian Raid, volunteered in defence of their country, and who drilled under considerable difficulty and at very considerable expense to themselves, and whose case has been refused consideration at the hands of this Government.
It is unfair; it is unjust. There are a number of men living in Prince Edward Island at present who at the time of the raid lived in Nova Scotia. These men have had their bounties, and in discussing the matter with their neighbours have admitted that at the time of the raid they did no more than the men on Prince Edward Island, in fact not even so much. I think nothing could be more unfair than this discrimination against Prince Edward Island, and I hope that the Government, even at this late date, will take the matter into consideration; and the Government should above all things he absolutely fair to all sections of the Dominion. There is no reason in the world why Prince Edward Island should be singled out for this unfair treatment, and I must enter my protest against it even at this late date.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: In Nova Scotia we have the clear records, but we have not been able to get clear records as regards Prince Edward Island. If it can be shown that any injustice had been done, or if we can get clear records as regards Prince Edward Island, I am sure that the Prime Minister and his colleagues will be glad to take the matter up.

We pointed out, when this matter was before Parliament last year, that the only difference between Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island was a technical difference. The men in Nova Scotia were called out by proclamation while the men in Prince Edward Island were called out by a special Act of Parliament passed by the local legislature. Surely a special Act of Parliament should be just as good.evidence as the proclamation calling out the men from Nova Scotia.

Anything that the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) or the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Hughes) or I can do to strengthen the hands of the minister and his colleagues in trying to get this bounty paid to the widows of deceased veterans, we shall be very glad to do. One thing has been settled by this Government, and that is the principle that the Eenian Raid veterans are entitled to this recognition of $100 each; and the minister should have no trouble in keeping the Government up to that principle which they have already established and on which they have already paid out so much money. If there is any good reasoning at all about this payment of money-I am not finding fault with it-the money is paid on the principle that the veteran who came out and served his country has earned this money, that he is entitled to this $100 because at	the	time	of the raidhe volunteered and put himself in a position to	defend	his country.
According to that principle the volunteer has earned the money as soon as he has rendered that service. Now whether he dies early in life or late does not alter the position at all, because it is the act of bravery and sacrifice that he performed for his country in 1866 that has given rise to this right for himself or for his family. The fact that he died before the first day of April 1912 cannot change that principle at all. The Government has thought proper to pay the bounty to the widows of men who died since the first day of April, 1912. They are paying the bounty to the widows and heirs of veterans who served in 1866,

and were living on the first day of April 1912, but died before they got the bounty. I wish to bring home to the minister if I can, that as far as sound reasoning is concerned, the widow of the man who died two years ago has mo better right to this money than the widow of the man -who died four years ago. That is a mere accident of time, a mere accident of a long or a short life; iand that is all the difference between the two. If the widow of the man who died last summer is entitled to this money and has got it, should not the bounty be also given to the widow of the man who died three or ten years ago, or at any time since he put himself in a position to be entitled to this money? I think that is fair, and sound logic. The minister should put all the widows and all the veterans in the same class, no matter whether some of the veterans happened to die some months or years before this Act was passed on the 1st day of April, 1912.

I am glad to have the opportunity of raising my voice on behalf of those widows who I think are unjustly discriminated against. I have had the honour of presenting to the Minister of Militia a petition signed by about one hundred petitioners from the county I have the honour to. represent. It seems to me these widows are just 'as much entitled to the bounty as those who have received it. The argument put up by my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Air. McKenzie) covers the ground so well that I have nothing further to say, except to express my hope that the minister will see his way to doing this act of justice.

That letter was written on the 25th November. The matter was brought to the attention of the House some four weeks ago, and the minister informed me that the cases in which the owners of the land had refused the compensation offered them had been placed in the Department of Justice and that the Department of Justice had taken or was taking proceedings to have the matter adjudicated in court. A discussion took place on the matter in this House about the 1st fii March, and on the 5th of March, I received from Mr. Cannon a letter in which he states:	.
I have read with great interest the debate which took place the other day between you and Colonel Hughes on the subject of the manner in which the farmers of Valeartier are treated.
I represent Frank McLaughlin, Hugh Bowles, Madame Veuve Conway, Thomas Thompson, Michael Woodlock and Joseph Griffin, and notwithstanding all my efforts I have not yet succeeded in having proceedings in the Exchequer Court to fix the amount of the indemnity.
I replied to Mr. Cannon, whom I know very well, asking him if I was to understand that up to that date nothing had been done before the Exchequer Court, and on the 10th of March he wrote me:

I have received your letter of the 8th, and I must tell you again that notwithstanding all my efforts we have not yet succeeded in obtaining the least satisfaction, and that no proceedings out of the Court of Exchequer have yet been served upon my clients.
On the 25th of November last, the department was asked to have the matter started at,once in the Exchequer Court, and up to the 10th of March no proceeding had yet been taken. I ask the Minister of Militia and I ask the Government if such negligence is not almost criminal? These people are in fair circumstances, but they are not millionaires, and having been deprived of their land they should have been paid compensation long ago, or the matter should have been promptly taken to the Court. Mr. Cannon, who belongs to one of the'leading law firms in the province of Quebec, represents seven or eight of these people. Yesterday morning I received a letter from another party, who was not a client of Mr. Cannon's, appealing still more and bringing a very sad case to my notice. I am sorry to say that it must reflect very severely upon the administration of the department. This is the letter I have received :
Valeartier Village, Que.,
March 23, 1915.
To Sir Wilfrid Laurier:
Sir,-I am taking the liberty of addressing you on behalf of my own family with regard to this land which is being taken up for the " Artillery Camp.", Our land is 120 acres and runs up to the camp ground from the Valeartier road, 75 acres or so being in a line with those large mountains, which part we agreed to sell at a moderate rate.
My husband's people have owned this land for a century, and, although it is not a model farm, have made a living on it. On Septemoer 4, 1914, the agent in charge of the camp sent a gang of men and tore down our fences, even a garden patch; and as the crop was not taken up, it was completely destroyed by the horses and cattle, while we were ordered to keep our cattle in the barn away from the shooting range. Now we have not received one cent for all this damage and have had to buy feed for our cattle at present rates. We have a family to keep, school, clothe, etc., and as last spring my husband had to go through a very dangerous and expensive operation in hospital, we cannot afford to lose our last year's crop. I am sure this matter has not been investigated by proper authorities or we would never be so abused.
The spring coming so soon and nothing settled leaves a poor lookout for us farmers. For confirmation of my statements I refer you to Mr. A. Robertson, K.C., 61 St. Peter street, Que. He has our bill and understands the case.
I am, yours very respectfully,
(Sgd.) Mrs. Rich. Smith.
To-day is the 26t.h of March. This is a poor family whose property has been ex-

propriated. Must I appeal to the 'sensibilities and the good feeling of my hon. friend the minister ? He should take this case to heart and see that those people at once receive what is their fair due. This family is in sad circumstances through the sickness of the bread-winner; the wife .appeals to me, and I appeal to the minister that this outrage should not be perpetrated any longer.
