The Crown has very extraordinary powers with regard to expropriation of land for public purposes, and those powers are necessary. By a mere filing of a plan and description in the registry office, the title of the occupant and the titles of all persons interested become absolutely vested in the Crown. In addition to that, it is not competent for the person in occupation of the land to take any proceedings himself, because under a statute amending the former Expropriation Act, -which was passed fourteen or fifteen years ago, the proceedings must be instituted by the Crown. I therefore entirely agree that there should be prompt action when a man's property is taken and the price cannot be agreed upon. In some of those cases there was a price agreed upon, and afterwards the person who had orally

or otherwise agreed to accept a certain figure thought that he was entitled to more. That would naturally be a reason for some delay. I take the view, however, that when it is once definitely ascertained that a price cannot be agreed upon between the Crown and a person whose land is being expropriated, then there should be no delay whatever in getting the matter to the Exchequer Court, because until the matter has been settled there, the man cannot obtain his money. Therefore I hope there will be no further delay in putting into the Exchequer Court the ease of any man whose property is expropriated, when there is any difference of opinion as to the price. I can assure my right hon. friend that, being impressed by that view, I will take some personal interest in the matter and confer with my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and with the Department of Justice, and ascertain the reasons for the delay and see that there shall not be further unnecessary delay in getting these matters settled.

I am very glad to hear from the Prime Minister that he will take an interest himself in these matters. I know very well that there are differences of opinion and that sometimes a man may be asking too much. In any such case, the matter should be at once put into the Exchequer Court.

I would not ask the indulgence of the committee, even for a few minutes, were it not that I desire to, correct a curious error which my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) fell into last night. I was not present when he commenced his speech, but I have had an opportunity of reading it in Hansard. He produced a number of affidavits which he read to the committee. It will be remembered by hon. members who have taken an interest in the discussion about the 17th Regiment of Nova Scotia, that I read a memorandum a few days ago signed by a number of soldiers who had been connected in some way with the 17th Battalion. This memorandum purported to corroborate the statements made by the Morning Chronicle, and to be signed by these gentlemen. I ivish to make it clear to the House and to the Minister of Militia that I had nothing to. do with the preparation of that memorandum. It was sent to me by Mr. Crowell, a reporter of the Morning Chronicle. In justice to Mr. Crowell, I thought it proper to lay it before the committee. The hon. member for Cumberland comes on [Sir Robert Borden.l
with a long list of affidavits from soldiers whose names were not on the memorandum. Why he produced these affidavits I find it difficult to understand. The first affidavit is from Robert Aldridge, of Toronto. He tells us a long story about Spas Stackoff, who, it appears, signed a paper and got a cigar for signing it. I do not know who Robert Aldridge is. He is not one of thfi men who signed the paper which I presented to the House-he does not figure in that paper at all. The next affidavit read by my hon. friend is by Mr. Stackoff himself. He tells a long story, and says he signed a paper and got a cigar. But he did not sign the paper I presented. The only document before the committee with the name of Stackoff on it is the one presented by the hon. member for Cumberland. I can only assume that Mr. Stackoff must have got a cigar for signing that 'paper.
I never saw this interesting memorandum to which the hon. gentleman refers. Has he the memorandum?
I haven't it here.
Can the hon. member get it?
I can.
The original?

The original is in Mr. Crowell's hands. I can get it for my hon. friend. A correct copy of it is in Hansard, and if the hon. gentleman will refer to it he will find that his friends, Stackoff and Aldridge, are not named there. So, they could not have got a cigar for signing that memorandum. The name on the next affidavit is William Thomas Oldridge, of London, Ontario. My hon. friend may know who he is; I do not. This gentleman says that Mr. Stackoff could not read. That is interesting information in itself, but I do not see how it concerns the House at this time. He says also that Stackoff signed a document and got a cigar. But William Thomas Oldridge did not sign the memorandum that I submitted to the House. If he got a cigar for signing a document it must have been for signing the affidavit submitted by the hon. member for Cumberland. These soldiers seem to have received cigars for signing papers. But as they did not sign the paper I submitted to the House,
I cannot see any .reason for reading these affidavits. The next affidavit is by Albert Harris, of Toronto.	This is
another man whom I never heard of before and whose name does not ap-

pear on the document I submitted. I do not wish to weary the committee going over the matter, but I want to point out that my hon. friend could not have read the memorandum sent to me by Mr. Crowell or he would not have read these affidavits.
Also, I would point out that at the time when he was dealing with these affidavits, the hon. gentleman must have had in his possession the letter of his friend Colonel Struan Robertson. He must have known what that hon. gentleman said in regard to these matters. It does not interest us very much what these other men from other parts of the country did or did not know about it. There are also two men from my hon. friend's constituency, Captain Bent and Captain Cutten who signed the memorandum read by my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte.) If, as I understand, these men come from Cumberland, my hon. friend (Mr. Rhodes) will probably know them and know whether they are men to be depended - upon or not. We have statements from them similar to those published in the Morning Chronicle at the time, and I would like to know whether or not we can depend upon anything they say.
I do not wish to delay the committee, but the whole difficulty seems to have arisen from the appointment of Colonel Struan Robertson to the command, an'd the only man responsible for that is the Minister of Militia. The minister, I understand, passed over other men who were entitled by seniority to the position which Mr. Robertson got. Mr. Robertson was a competent man, or he was not a competent man. If he was competent, the Minister of Militia should have stood by him and helped him through; if he was not competent the minister should have dismissed him and put a competent man in his place. That, it appears to me, is the whole story. It is for the minister to explain why this man failed so badly in the management of the Nova Scotia battalion. When he found that Colonel Robertson was not getting along very well in the position in which he had placed him and that he had not enough men to form a battalion, he should have sent for him, taken him into his tent, talked it over with him and assisted him to send back to Nova Scotia to recruit men. Men could easily have been had. The proof of that is that since that date a regiment has been recruited in that province. If the minister had stood by Colonel Robertson there would have been no trouble about it. He seems
to have got into an altercation and into trouble with him. It is not for me to explain that. He should have done one' thing or the other-he should have stood by Colonel Robertson loyally and made the battalion a success, or he should have dismissed him and put one of the other men who, I am told, are competent men, in his place, so that the battalion would have had a chance to be of service to the country. That is the whole question, and it seems to me that the Minister" of Militia has not yet given us a satisfactory explanation of this matter.

Knowing the persistency of the hon. member for Guysborough, I should be the last person in the world to enter into a verbal controversy with him in this committee, because I could never expect to succeed in having the last word. But he has made one or two remarks to-day which, I think, call for a few words from me. It is unfortunate that the hon. gentleman should continue from day to day to mention this matter even in a mild and brief way, because it serves only to accentuate the feeling of disquietude and unrest on the part of the friends at heme of those who are now at the front. The hon. member for Guysborough can serve but one purpose in bringing this matter to the attention of the committee, and that is the making of political capital for himself and his friends in the province of Nova Scotia.
The person chiefly concerned in this matter is the hon. gentleman's own political friend.

The hon. member for Guysborough, in common with other hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, fail utterly to grasp the significance of this question. If there is anything in it at all, it is a matter respecting the regiment concerned and the province which it represents. I say respectfully but sincerely that the fact that there are in this matter considerations above and beyond Major Struan Robertson or any other individual or group of individuals, seems to be too comprehensive to be grasped by the hon. gentleman's intellect. The point at issue is a matter affecting not particularly Major Struan Robertson, or Brown or Smith, but a regiment representing a province; I say this without the least desire to give offence to the hon. member for Guysborough. The hon. member is entirely too sensitive; he apparently thinks that any remarks which I made in regard to this matter last night were addressed particularly to himself.
Oh, no.

Or t,o his memorandum. It. was quite open t.o me to read the affidavit of Stackoff or of any other person which had particular reference to the matter under discussion. The hon. member for Guysborough admits that he read to the committee what purported to be a copy of the memorandum, the original of which is in the hands of Mr. Crowell of the Halifax Chronicle. I think it is incompetent and unfair for the hon. member to say that the memorandum which he read is a fair copy unless he has seen the original, and having compared it with the one in his possession, is thereby enabled to make that assertion. While I was not present when these affidavits were prepared, I have every reason to believe that while they were made by men whose names did not appear upon the memorandum read by the hon. member for Guysborough. They may have been made by men who signed the memorandum which was the original of the one read by the hon. member for Guysborough, some of the names on which had been erased. They may have been made by men who signed statements which were used in Halifax and which possibly appeared in the Halifax Morning Chronicle. But the argument of the hon. member was purely specious. If he will look carefully at his memorandum he will find" that these names were mentioned in it: H. Clarson; David Walters, of Cayuga, Ont.; H. Dobson, 577 La Salle road, Verdun, Montreal; W. H. Stearn, Lakehurst, Ont. I read affidavits signed by each of these four men, and I submit that this was perfectly good and competent evidence for me to submit.
I wish to correct the hon. gentleman: Walter Stearn, of Peterborough, not W. H. Stearn, of Lakehurst, Ont., was the man whose affidavit was read.

There may be some difference in the addresses, but my impression is that W. H. Stearn, whose affidavit I read last night, is the same man whose name is said to appear in the memorandum read by my hon. friend. To continue this discussion from day to day can serve no useful purpose, unless, possibly, that of gaining some small political advantage. I say possibly, because I do not believe that you can make small political capital out of 'a big question like this. And I believe that the people of the province of Nova Scotia are

patriotic enough, big-minded and broadminded enough, not to be misled by any small side issues which may be brought up while a great world war is taking place. It would be far better to leave this matter in abeyance until the men return from the front, because we cannot submit competent proof of the truth or falsity of the various statements until they do return. In the meantime, I think we ought to put our shoulders to the wheel, forget these small differences, and let the matter rest quietly. The Morning Chronicle, I think, made a very serious mistake-I say this not from a partisan standpoint-in publishing Mr. Crowell's letter, and those who read that paper observe that they regret the publication of that letter, because they are climbing down gracefully. But let us forget that. I am sure that if hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House will let the matter rest quietly, we on this side will do the same. I am not authorized to speak for the Minister of Militia and the Government, but I am sure that they are most anxious that the fullest and most complete inquiry shall be made into this whole affair when the proper time arrives.

No man likes the quiet life more than I do, but I wish to point out to my hon. friend that he misled the committee last night-not intentionally, I suppose-in reading these affidavits, because many hon. gentlemen supposed that they were made by the same men who had signed the memorandum which I had read to the committee, that these men signed the memorandum for a cigar, and that they did not know what they were signing. It turns out, however, that the great majority of the men whose affidavits were read by the hon. gentleman were not the same men at all, and that they had not signed the memorandum to which I referred. That was my reason for bringing up the matter again this afternoon, and I think my hon. friend will appreciate my attitude in the matter, because I do not think he would wish to leave a wrong impression upon the minds of hon. gentlemen of the committee.

What was the reason
which led to the purchase and fitting up of Valcartier camp", and what did it cost?

The department has been for a number of years selecting manoeuvring points in the military divisions of the country. We have one at Medicine, Hat, one near Moosejaw, which

has not been used much as yet, one at Seweli, Manitoba, a small area in Toronto, the Petawawa camp and so on. We have camps in various military divisions in order to avoid the expense of transporting the troops for long distances'! A few years ago I pointed out to the House that in three years the cost of transporting the troops of each division to one central camp would pay the cost of these various manoeuvring areas. It was with the object of avoiding this expense that we looked up a manoeuvring area for Quebec.
Quebec being a very important summer seaport, it was deemed advisable to select the area as near the city as possible, and it has been generally conceded that the department was fortunate in securing the area at Valcartier. I have not the figures of the cost, but I shall be glad to furnish them.

I am to understand that
the camp at Valcartier was not purchased with any relation to the existing war conditions; it was merely in carrying out the ordinary policy of the department?
During the summer, before war broke out at all, we had taken a portion of the land; then, when the war broke out, we took the balance of the present area.

I wish to have it thoroughly understood that the purchase of the camp ait Valcartier was in pursuance of the general policy of the department and had no relation to the existence of war conditions. Therefore I presume it is paid for out of the'ordinary militia appropriation.
In regard to rifle ranges, I should like to impress upon the minister, what perhaps is not necessary, that at a time like the present, when it is desirable that there should be an expansion of military knowledge, of which the most essential part is the use of the rifle, the department might very well give special attention to the securing and the fitting up of rifle ranges for the use not only of the enrolled militia but also of the civilian population who take an interest in rifle practice. At Edmonton the Government possesses a rifle range in a convenient situation which has not been in use and has not been replaced. I think it most important that if that range is not available it should be replaced by some other range. There is a large centre of population there, a large number of people who desire to practise rifle shooting, partly as a measure of amusement and partly as a military pre-98
paration. They have been debarred from doing so during the strenuous conditions that have existed during the past six months. Has the minister had in hand the securing of a convenient rifle range in the vicinity and what progress has been made and what are the prospects there?

I am glad the hon. member has brought this matter up and by his criticism has given me support in this matter. We have a rifle range at Edmonton, but it is right in the city, and there are houses right in the line of fire. While there is not any legal process which prevents us from using it, it is not what we call a safe range, and therefore we did not feel inclined to use it on account of the danger. We had selected a site eight or nine miles south of Edmonton, but there was no means of getting there unless we chartered a train every time we wanted to take men to the range. I was assured that there was a probability of a street car line being extended to the west of the city out towards the Indian reserve, and I would like to have my hon. friend look over the map with me sometime, when I would point out to him two or three places we have had in mind. The only objection to them
5 p.m. is that at present they are inaccessible. My officers have looked around Edmonton in every direction. Between Edmonton and Fort Saskatchewan the land is very dear, and down the valley it is practically all in use for other purposes. North of the city we have no proper land. I would be glad to receive any suggestion from the hon. gentleman, because it is a very important matter. We can sell the range we now have in Edmonton, even at a fair price, which would more than pay for a very extensive range.

While the range now owned by the Government is within the city limits, there has not been such an increase in building in the line of fire as would lead one to believe that the range was unduly dangerous. I quite appreciate that it is within the city limits with buildings liable to be erected within the line of fire, and that it is not desirable that this range should be considered a permanent one; but I certainly do think that during the past half year, when considerable interest was taken in militia matters, a special case might very well have been made for the opening of rifle practice upon that range. I really think that the militia authorities



have not shown that interest in the matter that they might very well have shown. As to what may be done in the spring, I would still urge on the minister a careful examination of the existing range and of the ground likely to be dangerously occupied in its neighbourhood. If arrangements could be made that would allow rifle practice to be carried on with a reasonable degree of safety until such time as the department might be able to secure another convenient range, it would be a distinct advantage. It must be remembered that this particular range is very conveniently situated and that there is no possibility of getting another as conveniently situated. Therefore, there is an object in using that range if on careful examination it is found to be practicable. I am a little afraid that when that range was rejected the rejection was made rather because of real estate speculation than because of the actual circumstances of the case; and as real estate speculation is not as buoyant as it was, possibly, on reexamination, the decision of the department might be reversed.

We are not negligent in the matter. Not only have I had the engineers of the department examine the locality, but I have examined it myself. In the line of fire there are within one and a half miles of the rear of the target twenty or thirty houses, if not more. The rule is that a range to be safe must have a 400-foot hill or embankment in the rear, or a 2,500 yards area free of houses. At Bisley a few years ago, during rifle practice, a child was killed who was standing 5,000 yards in the rear. The bullet glanced from the frozen ground and struck her. If the hon. member will just try to picture a distance of 2,500 yards-and a bullet will easily go that distance-he will see that at the place he speaks of a bullet might very easily go right out to his own property, or if it were shot in the other direction thirty or forty houses would be right in the line of fire. I know that an agitation was got up at the time, and I think it was due to the very thing that my hon. friend speaks of. The place is quite unsafe for a range. Our engineers have examined it, and I have looked at it myself on two occasions within the last year and a half. The hill is not 400 feet high; it is only 190 feet.

It would not be profitable for me to argue with the minister, but my understanding of the situation is not identical with his. I do not think that there are
	'	,
houses behind, as my ' hon. friend says. However, all I ask is that a re-examination be made of the place to ascertain the actual facts, not with a view to using it as a permanent range, but simply as a temporary expedient, so that those who desire to have rifle practice may be able to gel it, pending the securing of an adequate range. I understand that the range at. Port Saskatchewan is in much the same position, and I would ask that it be re-examined too, with a view to its being used in the spring as a temporary range until a permanent one can be secured. I quite appreciate that the securing of a permanent range is a very serious matter.

If the hon.
member knows aiiy safe range near Edmonton that would do for the time being, I shall be glad to rent it in order that the boys can get practice during the coming weeks. I would send out my engineers right away.
I would certainly appreciate it very much if the minister could locate temporary ranges. I know that a large number of people are eager to get rifle practice.

I do not wish to interfere with the more important work of the committee, but there is a matter which I have already brought to the notice of the minister in regard to military matters in my part of the country, and which I feel I should not be doing my duty to myself, to my constituents or to the public generally if I did not bring it publicly to the notice of the Minister of Militia and of the Prime Minister. In the part of the Dominion from which I come I am proud to -say that we have responded in the most hearty manner to the call of- our country in respect to everything that could be done to show our desire to assist in the strenuous fight that the country is now putting up not only for its own protection, but lor the protection of every part of the Empire. We are always glad to assist in whatever is going on in our part of the country in furthering that cause. I must complain to the minister that while sons of all families, irrespective of politics, were coming out, whenever any little favour was to be shown, whenever a dollar was to be spent or anything done that would be of any profit, then the party line was drawn as rigidly and as closely as ever it could be drawn; and I wish to bring home to the minister that he and everybody under him connected with that matter were of the narrowest possible kind ol partisans. For that alone,

however, I would not bring this matter up; but when militarism, and partyism, and Toryism get together for the purpose of interfering with the administration of justice in the High Couit of Justice in the province of Nova Scotia, it is time that the people of this Dominion should know where such interference comes from, and whether it is going to be tolerated. During last November, I think it was, a very serious and important action was being tried in the county of Victoria. A man in the militia was an important witness in the case. A subpoena was served upon him and his conduct money given to him at the city of Sydney. I was counsel in tne case, and I went to the colonel in command and said as respectfully as I could; " There is a man in your camp here who is a witness in an important case in the county of Victoria. He has been served with a subpoena from the Supreme Court and has been given his conduct money, and I hope you will let him go." xie positively told me, " No, I will not let him go." He knew what the case was, he knew it was an election trial, and he was a Tory himself. He told me bluntly, " I will not let him go." "We then took steps to get an order from the omcer at Halifax, whose name I forget, but he was a gentleman, fie issued an order that this man should attend the court under escort, that the escort should take him there and bring him back. That was perfectly satisfactory, and, I presume, according to the proper rules of the service. But the other officer was not to be outdone. He learned that this order had been issued over his head, and what did he do? He gave orders that the man should leave camp in civilian clothes, and the man was taken in charge by some Tory henchmen and stolen out of the country and landed in St. John's, Newfoundland. He was kept there for fully a week until they thought the trial was over. Then the men who stole him out of the country and took him to Newfoundland thought it was safe to leave him. They left the man, and he came back to Canada. We found out that he had returned and sent officers after him. We put him on the stand and he told his story. He told the story that he was stolen from the camp, and that he went out in civilian clothes by order of the officer in charge. They never looked for him; they knew where he was, and that there were parties who were going to steal him out of the couniry so that he should not give evidence. But he gave evidence on oath, which is a matter of record in the province, 98i
how he was stolen out of the country, and how he was permitted to leave camp. His name is Walter Tickner. Why was he wanted as a witness? He was wanted because during a certain election in the county of Victoria he was sent as pilot with four personators. These four personators were taken from the county of Cape Breton into the county of Victoria for the purpose of voting. They had no business to vote; it was well known they had not a vote in the county of Victoria, but these four men who were strangers in the county were guided by this fellow to a place called Middle River, where they swore falsely to certain names and voted. The man then took them to North Gut, where again they swore falsely to certain names and voted. They voted twice on the same day. This man Tickner was required as a witness in the election trial, but the Tory machine, headed by Mr. Douglas, Mr. Muirhead and Dr. Hayes, stole him out of the country. The officers of the militia were hand in glove with them and helped them to take him out of the country, and they tried, if possible, to prevent him giving evidence before the Supreme Court of our province. I wrote that to the minister very shortly after the. trial, but from that day to this I am not aware that the slightest action has been taken. The officers who were parties to stealing this man out of the country are still in charge as they were, and I never heard there was any complaint made about them. When conduct of that kind is committed by a minister of the Crown, by colonels and officers and generals in this country, and an attempt made to carry out small, dark, dirty politics, I think it is my duty, standing in this House, to let the country at large know what the Premier knows, that - that is the way some of the money voted here is being used, and that instead of being used for the defence of the country it is used for defending the low intrigues of such men as Dr. Hayes, J. C. Douglas, M.P.P. and Mr. Muirhead. I say I would not be doing justice to this great country, and I would not have a proper conception of the administration of justice in this country, if I did not bring this matter to the attention of the House.

I received a communication from the hon- member (Mr. McKenzie), and I immediately asked for a report. The report furnished to me was that this soldier had been sent on some mission and had been absent for some time, and

that he returned and' gave evidence on the trial. If my "memory serves me right, I was informed that the officer in charge was one of the staunchest Liberals in the country, a gentleman by the name of Major McLean. I do not know whether I am talking by the card or not, but the report to me was along these lines; that is, from the military view point, and I do not let political squabbles interfere at all in these matters. The soldier, on the occasion of my visit, happened to be the sergeant of the guard, I remembered his name, having heard it from my hon. friend, and I made further inquiries from the military view point, and I was told on that occasion that there had been nothing irregular, that the order had been given from Halifax in proper form, and that before the order was received the man had been sent on his mission. I was -assured at the time that the officer in command was one of the staunchest of Liberals, and a supporter of my hon. friend.
_ Mr. McKENZIE: The Minister of Militia is certainly misled on that point, because this man came into Major McLean's command a long time after the trial was over and after he had come back from Newfoundland. But, when he was serving in Sydney and >vhen he was spirited out of the country, he was under the charge of Colonel McRae. Major McLean had nothing to do with him until a long time after the trial was over.

There are about one hundred men stationed at Canso, N.S., protecting the cable station, and when I was at Canso last fall j was 'informed that these young men had no opportunity to practise rifle shooting. I was told they had made application to the department to be allowed to do some rifle shooting, and I thought it would be very desirable if their request were acceded to. I wrote the minister at the time and he was kind enough to reply that he was having the matter looked into. Have any steps been taken to establish -a rifle range there, so as to enable these young men who are guarding the cable station, to practise shooting?

I have taken steps at all these 'Stations where there are troops to have them allowed from 50 to 75 rounds per man for practice. In some places rifle shooting is dangerous, and we must first look to 'the safety of the people. Canso is one of the places I was unable to visit when I was in the Maritime Prov-

inces, but I was ait Sydney Mines, North Sydney, Glace Bay, and other places. I was ishocked to see the places in which our soldiers were obliged to stay. They were as fine-looking a lot of soldiers as one could find in the wide world; splendid-looking fellows and well up in their drill. The places they slept in were ill-lighted, and without water or baths, and I immediately gave orders that there should be electric lights and water and baths installed. The order was a general one, and I presume it was carried out in Canso.
There are throughout the country schools for training officers, and not being a military man I would like the minister to explain what results are expected from these training schools.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That, will all be found in yesterday's Hansard.

A great many boys have gone to the front .and we want officers for the regular militia.and for the corps that are to be raised, and these officers have to be trained. We take any young man who is a militiaman, and if he is not a militiaman we male him one, if he is sound mentally and physically, we give him an opportunity to train. Xnese schools are turning out a lot of fin} boys all over the Dominion, ready to take the places of the boys who have already gone to the front.
That is a very general statement, but as the information was given more in detail yesterday, I shall look at it, in Hansard.

It, is stated that a committee of the Cabinet was appointed to purchase supplies when the Minister of Militia was absent. Would the minister state if this committee is yet in existence, and of what ministers is it composed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have prepared the fullest information about That and will give it on the War Appropriation measure tomorrow.
Militia and Defence-training areas, $200,000.
In what localities are further training areas to be secured?

AVe have provided for them in British Columbia, but we have not located them yet. AVe have one in southern Alberta, but we want one in northern Alberta, and the same thing applies to Saskatchewan. AVe have one in Manitoba, but we want one in the

second military district, Toronto in time, and one in the first military district in time. The saving of transportation charges alone would in three years pay for these areas.
Mr.- OLIVER: In Alberta, at present the military training is being carried on at Calgary, which I should fancy is a very suitable location for concentrating troops. Has the Government secured a leasehold of the training area there, or under what conditions have they been able to use that property.

The training area is on the Indian reserve. The Indians offered us a lease of several sections of land; but, as there were certain little difficulties in the way on account of other claims, we have not yet received a permanent release of the Piegan Indian reserve. There is on the reserve a range and a manoeuvring area that we shall be able to hold for 99 years. The Indians are willing; but there are conditions, of which I do not know the details, which prevent us from consummating the deal. It is, however, a long haul from Lloydminster and from the boundaries of Alberta and Saskatchewan to Calgary, and that means many thousand dollars a year. When we get a troop area, all the troops in the north, as the different bodies gradually develop, can be brought to some home locality for training.
I rather understood the minister to say a little while ago that there was a training area in Alberta near Medicine Hat?
Just north of Medicine Hat.
I wondered what was the connection, because I had not heard of troops being trained in that area.

There was no railway there last year, and we would have had to go 30 miles without a railway. There is now a railway. The area may do for the whole of Alberta. The troops can go down those diagonal lines from the northern parts of Alberta to that range. We have not looked fully into the matter yet.

If it is possible to make an arrangement for a training area, it would be very much more desirable than the area my hon. friend speaks about, because it is not near Medicine Hat, although it is in the Medicine Hat district.
It is 30 miles north of Medicine Hat.

It is on a single line of railway, not at a point where lines come together. I quite appreciate the desirability of securing an area in the north country as well as in the south. I would be glad to see that done, but I think it should always be done with regard to convenience of location; that is, convenience for the bringing together of the different bodies of troops, if a considerable area can be secured at such a point, as it can be at Calgary.
Pensions payable to militiamen on account of the rebellion in 1SS5, and active service generally, flOO.OOO.
Is this in relation to pensions already earned, or has it any relation to pensions to be earned?
These pensions are payable to militiamen on account of the rebellion in 1885.
Is any provision made in the Estimates for pensions for soldiers disabled in the present war?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That will be a matter for the Supplementary Estimates.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ["No, I have heard no charges whatever.\nAt six o'clock, the House resumed, and then took recess.\nThe House resumed at eight o'clock. PRIVATE BILLS."]
Has a special immigration officer or publicity agent been appointed for eastern Nova Scotia?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: A petition was received yesterday or to-day, and is in my office, asking for the appointment; but it has not been given the consideration necessary, and no appointment has been made.
And the hon. minister cannot state whether he will make the appointment or not?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
think it essential? He is better acquainted with the province than I am. I should like. to have the benefit of his opinion.

I am surprised to hear that it is only now the hon.-minister is aware of the necessity of such a publicity agent. There was a petition over a year ago, backed by resolutions of the Boar3 of Trade and the Forward Movement Association; and I called the attention of the minister last year to the desirability of such an appointment being made. The hon. gentleman said then that he would give it favourable consideration. It is rather surprising to find that he does not seem to know anything about this matter except that a petition has just come in. There were representations made from all over the country, not only from Antigonish, but from the several towns in eastern Nova Scotia, and backed by many men of standing and prominence in that part of the country, urging this appointment. The files of the department are loaded down with corre-

spondence on this subject. Not only was the minister importuned, but the acting minister in his absence, -and the Prime Minister and others have been urged to make this appointment. It seems strange that the minister is not aware of the necessity and desirability of such an appointment being made. All that I can say'is that my remarks, made when the Estimates were going through last year with reference to this question, will be found on Hansard. It was then stated, as strongly as I could state it, that it was desirable that an energetic, wide-awake agent should be appointed.
An unfortunate thing is that the rural districts have lost population, particularly the county I have the honour to represent, this being due to the fact that the West was so extensively advertised. The effort is now being made to have the vacant farms taken hold of by the native-born and by immigrants from across the water. Of course, I suppose, just now we cannot expect very much in the way of immigration from Europe. But there are a great many of our native sons living in the West who would very quickly come back to the East, and the time, I think, is very opportune for the work of an energetic publicity agent who would bring to the notice of our own people as well as others not only the possibilities but the advantages offered by the farms of the East. I hope the minister will be able to say something a little more definite than that the matter is under consideration and that he has had it under consideration for only a few days.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is not often that hon. gentlemen opposite condemn a minister for not making sufficient appointments. The criticisms to which we are subject are usually on the opposite line. Of course, in the multiplicity of applications hon. gentlemen cannot expect that I should have this one that has been mentioned by the hon. member for Guysborough immediately in mind and that I should recollect just what took place a year ago. But the matter is fresh in my mind by reason of the fact that there is a petition on my desk which I have recently received and to which I have not had time to give the consideration it deserves. That does not necessarily mean, of course, that I will not pass favourably upon it. I am glad to have had the opinion of the hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. . Chisholm) as to the desirability of having such an appointment. The only reason why I would hesitate is that I have to endeavour

to economize 'by not making more new appointments than are absolutely necessary. As the hon. gentleman says, there will not be very much overseas immigration this year. There may be immigration from the United States, although we expect that that also will fall off. That is one reason why I do not care to multiply the officials if I can possibly avoid it. At the same time, if I am impressed with the idea that in any particular province there is necessity to have another official publicity agent as the hon. gentleman suggests, and it falls within the purview of our department to make such an appointment, I have no objection to favourably consider it.
Do I gather from what the minister says that it is the intention to appoint a publicity agent to induce immigration from various parts of this country to other parts?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, the work is more that of repatriation. I think the petition that I read this mornipg dwells upon the idea of inducing immigrants from outside of Canada to come to the province of Nova Scotia. There have been some complaints-we had mention of 'it here to-day-that the attention of the Immigration Department has been more particularly devoted to Western Canada, and it is suggested that Nova Scotia probably has not had its due in that respect. It was not with the idea of running a publicity bureau alone, but of appointing an immigration agent for the province of Nova Scotia.
Perhaps the hon. minister will say what he meant by speaking of the repatriation of Nova Scotians who have gone West.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman misunderstood me; I was not referring to Nova Scotians who have gone West. There are a number of Canadians in the United States who might be repatriated.

I think it
is considered desirable that the province should be peopled with native-born persons; they understand the conditions peculiar to the province, make the best settlers, and are more desirable in every respect. I am sorry to hear the minister suggest that it is not intended that the publicity agent shall extend his operations to other parts of Canada with a view to inducing native-born Nova Scotians who are in the West to return to their own province. If the oper-
'ations of Mr. Webb are to be confined to the United States and to the Old Country, and if, as the minister alleges, there is a prospect of getting no immigrants from the old country and but few from the United States, I am afraid the minister has virtually admitted that there is little hope of this publicity agent being appointed in the near future.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's idea as to how the public funds should be expended in connection with immigration differs from mine. I do not think that the money of the people of Canada should be devoted to an effort to induce settlers in one part of the country to migrate to another. In fact, accusations were made in years gone by against the then Government that they were trying to induce eastern Canadians to migrate to the West. If Nova Scotians have gone West or to other provinces of Canada, they know the conditions both in the province they came from and in the province in which they have settled; and if dissatisfied they will go back; if contented, they will remain where they are. We are spending money on immigration with the idea of bringing settlers into Canada from other countries; not with the idea of inducing Nova Scotians to go West or persuading those who have gone West to return to the eastern provinces.
How many immigation agent's are there in Nova Scotia, under Dominion authority.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Three, I think. '

Do these agents act
as agents for the whole province, or is the province divided into districts?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: For the whole province.

I think the minister is perfectly right in saying that he is not justified in these hard times in creating offices. That is why I argued that he could dispose of a great many of the unnecessary officials who are in the various branches of the service, and use the money received by them to pay a live, wide-awake, energetic publicity agent. Last year I called attention to the fact that this Government sent several special agents from Nova Scotia, including one from my. own county, to Europe since 1911. They went off on a pleasure trip which lasted three months, and cost the country something like $6,000, and if my memory serves me. I think they receive $100 a month and expenses. Their report*

are on file, but if the minister can find in those reports anything useful to Canada's immigration policy or tending to increase immigration into this country, he will do more than I have been able to do. If he will avoid appointing agents of this kind merely for political purposes, to satisfy those who have been disappointed in other respects, and devote the money to real publicity work, some good will be accomplished.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I should not want the hon. gentleman to leave the impression upon the committee that these officials were in any sense permanent immigration agents. It has been the policy of the department for many years to send delegates from the various provinces of Canada to the Old Country to act temporarily during the winter months as immigration agents. They are placed under the direction of Mr. J. Obed Smith, of the London office. He arranges in advance that they shall he at certain provincial towns at certain times, to meet the people and to give them information. Some of them act in the capacity of lecturers and give addresses on Canada. This is temporary work which is carried on during the winter months; I think the period is three months, or a little longer.
Mr. MeCRANEY: As a western man I do not fall in with the suggestion of the hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) that a propaganda should be carried on to induce Nova Scotians who live in the province of Saskatchewan to go back to Nova Scotia, The former chief justice, the Attorney General of our province, and the two candidates who have opposed me in previous elections, are all Nova Scotians. Nova Scotians are among the most successful men we have, and I am sure that no matter how great a propaganda were carried on, they would not return, not because they do not love Nova Scotia, but because they are doing so well in the West. Our province is almost dominated by Nova Scotians. When Nova Scotians complain that they have not enough influence in this Parliament by reason of reduction in their representation, I feel like reminding them of the great influence which they are acquiring the West.

I wish to direct the attention of the minister to a matter which I have previously referred to him by letter, but in respect of which I have had very little indication as to what action he intends to take. It is with respect to the

grievance of a large number of the settlers west of the city of Wetaskiwin. The district, is about 50 miles from a railway. At one time it was heavily timbered, but a fire depleted it of its merchantable timber of any considerable value. Settlers were allowed to go in there and take up homesteads. After clearing up the land and making improvements they found that the soil was not suitable for the successful raising of crops; thus they have been unable to acquire the amount of land necessary to entitle them to a patent. At the same time they have been unable to make a living. My attention was called to the grievance of these people and I made a trip out to the settlement to look into the matter personally. I found the country entirely unsuited for anything except, possibly, mixed farming. To make matters worse, there has been considerable interference by the man who has been in charge of the patronage in that district. According to the statement of the settlers, he has been interfering with the duties of the homestead inspector and the timber ranger. Timber rangers who have been sent by the local office to make inspections have reported in many cases that there are more than 25 acres of merchantable timber on these lands. The regulations appear to be rather vague as to what constitutes merchantable timber, and the settlers consider that they are under a very distinct grievance inasmuch as the inspector has set aside a great deal of timber as merchantable which they say is a hindrance and a nuisance rather than of any value. A number of inspections have been made and yet these men are in the condition that they cannot get any satisfaction from the department other than the statement that they must fulfil the regulations and clear and crop 30 acres of land. This, in a district of this description, is practically impossible; and if they did carry out this condition the crops would not yield them any return. The district is better adapted for mixed farming and the raising and rearing of stock than the raising of grain. I wish to let the minister understand that political influences have been at work inasmuch as discrimination has been shown in favour of neighbours with the same amount of improvements in the granting of patents. Men who have done certain improvements have been allowed to get patents through the recommendation of the homestead inspector and the signs indicate that political influences have been brought to bear to bring

this condition about. I wish to point out to the minister the difficult and almost impossible condition that these settlers are in to clear and cultivate according to the regulations and, as I understand he has power as commissioner to alleviate these conditions in his own judgment, I think it would be wise for him to be as lenient as possible to the settlers in this district.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I believe that this question has engaged the attention of the officers of the department on several occasions. It appears that, as the hon. gentleman has said the settlers went into this district with their eyes open, and although there was abundance of prairie land open to be taken, they settled in a thickly timbered country where they could not make a living. It is true that fire had destroyed some of the timber. They took up homesteads contrary to the Dominion Lands Act by making affidavits at the land office that there was not more than 25 acres of timber on each area homesteaded. That is where they made their error. An inspector had been sent from the local office who reported more than 25 acres of timber. He set aside the 25 acres of timber, leaving them their homesteads, but leaving the other timber on the quarter-section to be utilized by settlers for permits. That was practically the only fair thing the department could do. They were not entitled to more than 25 acres of timber. The inspector set aside 25 acres. ' But they are not satisfied with that, 'they want to get their patents without doing the cultivation even although they cannot make their living on the quarter-section and they knew that before going on the land and they want to get all the timber to dispose of for commercial purposes. That is the way the case has been presented to me by the departmental officers. So far as politics is concerned, I know there have been some questions of that kind between the gentleman named and the particular man who is entering this complaint; but, as far as I can learn,, there is nothing in that, and the gentleman against whom the charges are made has sent us letters, which we have on file, absolutely denying that there has been anything of the kind.
Last session we passed an amendment to the Dominion Lands Act whereby on lands that have been taken up for homesteading on which the requisite amount of cultivation duties cannot he performed, patents may be secured by putting on a certain number of stock. That was not intended to be retroactive, but I am sure the department will look on this in a very
lenient manner, and if these gentleman cannot cultivate their lands, the department, I am sure, will have no objection to them qualifying for their patents by putting on a certain number of stock. What they object to is having the 25 acres of that timber land set aside for them and allowing the public to have permits to go in and take off the timber from the other portions of the quarter-section.
The minister will understand that the question comes in there as to what constitutes merchantable timber.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand that while there is no strict definition in regard to that, the department looks on timber above 10 inches in diameter as merchantable timber.
No matter whether it is poplar or spruce ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, if it is below 10 inches it can be used for firewood.
Speaking about polities in the department, has the minister heard any charges of political interference in connection with the opening up of the Duck Mountain timber reserve ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No, I have heard no charges whatever.

The House resumed at eight o'clock. PRIVATE BILLS.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
When the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney) moved for the papers, I hastily glanced over the file to acquaint myself more or less with the condition of affairs, and I found if very much as has been stated by the hon. gentleman. There is on the file considerable correspondence going to show that there was considerable feeling both for and against Mr. Schrader. Of course, Mr. Schrader claims that a good deal of the opposition to him getting the lease emanates from political opponents. The affidavit which was read would show that, inasmuch as it states that the secretary-treasurer of the council had vowed that he would see that the council passed resolutions against Mr. Schrader getting the lease. I say nothing about that.
There are rival applications for the grazing lease. I understand that an inspection was made of the land,1 and some was recommended to be given to one applicant and the balance to be given to Mr. Schrader. It was stated that it would be useless to give it all to the other gentleman by reason of the fact that he has not sufficient stock to stock it, nor means to purchase stock. On the other hand, it is represented by the inspector that Mr. Schrader has a good deal of thoroughbred stock and is in a position to stock, and has on another farm a good deal of stock.
It may be in his possession, but I doubt if it is in his own name.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I know nothing about that. At any rate, the department, owing to the conflicting applications, thought it desirable, though an inspection had been made, to bring in an outside and independent inspector who would not be prejudiced. He reported, I believe, that the lands upon the whole were not suitable 
for agriculture, though portions ware suitable, but that a good deal of the land was broken, stony and hilly, on the banks of the Saskatchewan. By reason of the fact that Mr. Schrader was in a better position to stock it, he recommended that Mr. Schradar be given the lease. However, as I understand it, Mr. Schrader did not comply with the license conditions in regard to the posting of notice for so many days. He was notified that he had to post for a certain number of days, and did post in one of the larger post offices on the line^ but did not comply with the strict regulations, and was so notified.	I do not think we have received notice stating whether he has complied with the conditions or not.
I can understand local feeling on this subject if it is contended that a great deal of this land is suitable for agriculture. The municipal council naturally desires to see the land taken up by homesteaders so that it can tax the land and. get a revenue. I have not passed upon the application, in the first place because no person had complied with the condition up to the date it was before me, and secondly because I thought that owing to the largely signed petition which we had received, we should go very slow before we grant a grazing lease in the face of such opposition. True, it was claimed by one signer that misrepresentations had been made to him or he would not have signed-it had been represented that it was the intention to fence off the ranch and shut him off from the river. But at any. rate I can promise the hon. gentleman that, I will look very carefully into the question and will not issue a grazing lease until I am convinced in my own mind that the land is not suitable for agriculture. Of course, I have always been desirous that land not guit-able for agriculture should not be settled upon; and I am more strongly convinced 'than ever that we should not throw opeu such land for agricultural occupation after our experience of this year, when we find that so much land is taken up by homesteaders on which they cannot make a living and that they come on the Government for seed grain. In view of these facts, I feel that we ought to be very careful about throwing ranching country open for settlement. It might suit these parties better to have a lot of smaller leases rather than have the land tied up for a series of years in the hands of one rancher. I will give the matter serious consideration and will be careful not to act prematurely.

I desire to ask the minister to make an independent inspection of the place I brought to his notice before dinner in regard to what constitutes merchantable timber. There is a very strong feeling in the district of Wetaskiwin that politics has entered into this case.
If the minister would put an independent timber ranger into that district and have him make an independent report, the fact of the case as brought out would probably vindicate the conduct of the present timber ranger. The feeling is very strongly held, however, by a large number of people, that political influence has been brought to bear upon the officials of the department in the reports which they have made. I would urge upon the minister that he secure an independent and impartial report of these particular cases, and satisfy himself as to whether these settlers are being fairly treated, or whether undue influence is being brought to bear upon the local officials -by parties interested.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If my memory serves me correctly, another inspection has already been ordered.
Only by the homestead inspector, d think.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am not certain of that.
] think the hon. member may disabuse his mind of the idea that the decisions given in these cases have been the result of political pressure unon the officials of the Government. My* officials are not of the political stripe which would permit them to be influenced by representations of that nature.
I mean the local officials.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The local officials have nothing to do with the decision; the " decision was made in the department by those who are responsible for it.

I want to say a word about the political aspect of this question. I had occasion to be in the neighbourhood of Wetaskiwin during the recess, and I found, amongst a number of the intelligent people of the district whom I met and conversed with, a very distinct impression that discrimination was being used in regard to the issuing of patents on political grounds. I desire to say that I entirely exonerate the minister from acting in such a manner. I know my. hon. friend well, and I am quite sure that he would not do anything at once so wrong and so silly. It would be very wrong, because, speaking from experience,
I can assure the minister, if he needs the assurance, that when a man has taken a homestead and has done honestly the work which entitles him to a patent, he is very anxious to have it and he has a right to have it. I am sure the minister recognizes that, and it would be a great wrong to the country if every reasonable expedition were not observed in the granting of the patent.
It would be silly, because we are not accustomed in this country to German methods. In Anglo-Saxon countries people do not respond to interferences with their freedom by supporting the Government that so interferes. I think that any such action, taken for political purposes would have a diametrically opposite effect to that which it was intended to have. If any man with an ounce of Anglo-Saxon blood in him, knowing that he was entitled to his patent, was refused it by the minions of a government simply because he did not vote as they wanted him to vote, he would vote twice as badly that way and get as many of his friends , as he could to do the same thing. I have found the impression prevailing that this motive was actuating the inspectors, and that is not the only neighbourhood in the province of Alberta in which I have found this impression existing since this Government came into power. My hon. friend, I feel sure, will be grateful to me for bringing this to his attention. I cannot recall-and I desire to divest myself of all partisanship in making this statement-ever having heard a complaint of that kind when the department was under the administration of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). I can recall complaints against the hon. member for Edmonton, but not that he ever advocated, practised or allowed discrimination on political grounds in such matters as these. I desire again to say that I exonerate the present minister from being actuated by any motive so petty. I am quite sure that if this thing is happening, it is happening at the instance of inspectors who are more zealous for party than they are for the interests of the country. Having brought the matter before the minister, I should like to suggest to him-he may think the matter over-that as a precautionary measure he should send a circular to all his inspectors, pointing out the wrongness and folly of making discrimination against any homesteader in regard to the issue of his patent.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman, being a medical man, knows human nature well enough to appreciate the fact that when a

man applies for his patent and thinks he ought to have it because he belongs to the party in power, he frequently blames his own friends when he does not get it. We have received considerable blame from some of our own political friends because we did not give them patents when they thought they were deserving of them, and when the officials of my department and myself saw that they had not complied with the homestead regulations and conditions. The hon. member may not have heard any complaints when the old Government was in power, but I would be more apt to hear such complaints than a supporter of the then Government, and I did hear any number of them- just such complaints as are made in this case.	They have always been
made, and they always will be made, no matter what	Government is in
power. The trouble is that many persons who take up homesteads desire to shirk their duties and to obtain their patents without complying with the regulations. Officials of the Interior Department pass upon nearly all applications; only occasionally-in complicated cases, where the officials do not desire themselves to take the responsibility -do applicants come before the minister. It is true that there may be some local officials who try to create the impression that they are in a position to have their recomendations carried out, but even homestead inspectors' recommendations are not carried out by the officials if they have evidence which leads them to believe that they should not adopt them. Frequently an outside inspector is sent into a district, to make an independent inspection. The^ officials did pass upon the particular case mentioned by the hon. member for Strath-cona; but the whole thing in a . nutshell is	that these people did not
comply with the homestead conditions. The hon. member says that they cannot cultivate sufficient acreage to carry out the homestead duties; that they went on land which i3 unfit for agricultural development. This being the case, how on earth can he expect the department to issue patents? The regulations are there, and must be complied with. We are not responsible for the fact that these people went on lands which cannot be broken up and cultivated. They can, of course, avail themselves of the stock provision. The report we have, however, is that these people went on that land for the purpose of utilizing the timber commercially. They feel that they have a grievance because they are only allowed 25 acres, but [Mr. Roche. 1
that is what the law prescribes. They wish to divest that land of timber and move on to another district, perhaps claiming another free homestead on the ground that the first was no good; in the meantime they will have lived off the timber. It is practically an impossibility for officials under the existing regulations to issue patents for these lands.

The minister will understand that timber fifty miles from a railway cannot be very valuable commercially. It is said that discrimihation is made as to the quality of merchantable timber which these different homesteads are said to con tain, and this is one of the causes of complaint on the part of the settlers. The question arises as to what is meant by merchantable timber. If the officials of the department were lenient in their interpretation of the expression " merchantable timber," I do not think there would be any trouble in this district. If fair play were given to all the settlers in the district, no complaint would be made. The statement is openly made, however, not by one person, but by many, that unfair discrimination is made as between one settler and another by the officials of the department. My desire is that an independent timber ranger should be sent to make a separate report as to what constitutes 25 acres of merchantable timber and as to whether it should be en bloc or picked out all over a man's farm. The minister can well understand that no man who wishes to make a living by keeping stock or in any other way *would wish his fences to be torn down to permit neighbours to go in and take timber off the land. I do not know that the settlers are asking anything unfair, they simply wish to be treated as their neighbours are. The minister can .see that a small official may make things very disagreeable for a whole settlement.
Do I understand that these gentlemen will be satisfied if they have their 160 acres with the timber on it ?
I think so. I never heard any complaint otherwise.
In what way would that improve the condition of the soil ?
It might enable them to raise stock. It would not improve the soii, but the land might be suitable for raising cattle.

I would remind the minister that a regulation in regard to timber which may be desirable and applicable- m

one condition is not desirable and should not be made applicable to another condition. Some years ago when the settlement was confined to what was called the prairie section of the West, an interpretation of merchantable timber would properly cover timber that was merchantable as firewood; but now that settlement has covered the prairie and has pushed back not only into the park country but into the heavy woods, as in the case mentioned by my hon. friend, but more particularly in the district which I represent, the interpretation that would be proper 100 miles to the south or east of Edmonton would be an entirely improper interpretation 100 miles north or west of Edmonton where the country is practically entirely timbered, with timber that 100 miles to the south or east would be considered very heavy-and yet that timber has no commercial value and must be cleared away at cost to the settler in order to enable him to cultivate the ground. Unless the department takes the view that timber must be preserved because it is timber, and I do not understand that they take that view, then I would add to what the hon. member for Stratheona has said, the suggestion that there should be a new interpretation put upon the words merchantable timber, applicable to those parts of the country where the country is covered with a growth of what would be called on the prairie heavy timber, but which in the heavily wooded country has really no merchantable value whatever. That is the condition which prevails throughout a very large part of the constituency I represent. As railroads are constructed through that territory and the settlers naturally push back along the railroad lines into the timber, this 'question becomes one of very pressing
9 p.m. importance. The minister has had a concrete case presented to him.
. What is the condition in isolated cases in Stratheona is the condition throughout a very large proportion of the much larger district of Edmonton, and the minister will find it very frequently in the administration of the land throughout that district. I therefore suggest that a new interpretation be placed on merchantable timber applicable to these conditions where the country is covered with a heavy forest growth but where those trees are not, by reason of conditions, of merchantable character.

I would like to bring to the attention of the minister an act of the department recently in the city of Lethbridge. Mr. A. E. Humphries, who had been an immigration official for some years, was relieved of office on the ground of economy. That was the explanation given to Mr. Humphries and the explanation which the minister gave to me this session. If that was the sole reason I would not be inclined to bring the matter to the attention of the House, because I am in favour of economy wherever it can be practised. Mr. Humphries was relieved from the positions of immigration inspector, immigration agent at Lethbridge, and caretaker of the immigration hall. But immediately after his removal, Mr. A. H. McKeown was appointed caretaker of the immigration hall at a salary of ,$65 a month, with plenty of accommodation for his family, which made the position a very good one for that gentleman. I think it would have been only fair to a servant of the character of Mr. Humphries that, if economy was to be practised, he should have 'been deprived of the other two positions but. have been allowed to retain the position of caretaker of the immigration hall. It is true that he was appointed by the late Government, but no charges were preferred against him that he was a partisan or an inefficient officer. Since this Government came into power they recognized his services and increased his salary, and officials of the department speak of him as one of the best immigration inspectors they had in the service, and he was recommended for an increase by the gentleman who at that time was in charge of the patronage in my riding for the Conservative party. There is no question that Mr. Humphries was an efficient officer, and I would like the minister to offer an explanation of his removal from all of these positions on the ground of economy, followed immediately by the appointment of a gentleman to the position of caretaker. I might say that within a very short time of Mr. Humphries being relieved of office relief was being distributed in southern Alberta. Mr. Humphries had had something to do in previous years with the distribution of relief in certain districts of Alberta. It was said that there was no work for him to do, that economy had to be practised. In my judgment, it would have been a wise act on the part of the Government to have given Mr. Humphries some of that work to do until the immigration business had improved, especially since the Government had recognized Mr. Humphries as an exceptionally good officer and had in-

creased his salary. But instead of that they appointed a gentleman from Lethbridge to the position of commissioner of relief at a salary of 1150 a month and Mr. Humphries, who was receiving less than that, was relieved on the ground of economy. If there had been any charge against him of inefficiency or partisanship I would not complain, but it is generally recognized by political friends of the minister that Mr. Humphries was one of the most capable officials in the department. That tribute was paid to him by Mr. W. C. Ives, who was handling the patronage in the riding of Medicine Hat and recommended him for an increase in salary,

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I know very little personally about this except that I recollect the question placed by the hon. gentleman on the Order Paper, and also that the following answer was given:
Owing to the fact there was at that time practically no work to do in connection with immigration at Lethbridge, Mr. A. E. Humphries was on October 15, 1914, indefinitely suspended from his position as travelling immigration inspector.
It does not say he was dismissed. It says lie was indefinitely suspended. The gentleman who took his place was appointed I think on the 1st January, 1915, on the strong representation of the Commissioner of Immigration that it would not do to have such a good building left without a caretaker. I do not know who this man is, but I understand he is getting $65 a month as caretaker. I think Humphries was getting $100 a month. Because this new man was appointed on the 1st January, 1915, it does not follow that Mr. Humphries was dismissed. Apparently there was no work for him to do. There was practically no immigration. And he is not the only official whose services have been temporarily dispensed with during this period of stress, and that applies to Conservatives too. I had to let off one of our inspectors in the Brandon district who was appointed by this Government. There was nothing against him; in fact, he was a first-class official; but his services were dispensed with on the ground of economy. The hon. gentleman might ask why Mr. Humphries was not appointed as caretaker. I cannot explain that; I do not even know whether he would have accepted it if it had been offered him. I think the best evidence that there was no partisanship about it is. the fact that his salary had been increased since this Government came into power.

The criticism I had
to offer was this. There might have been reason to abolish the position other than that of caretaker which Mr. Humphries was filling, but he had been caretaker and in charge of the Immigration hall at Lethbridge for years, and I cannot understand why, when he was removed from.the other offices, he should not have been allowed to retain the position of caretaker of the Immigration hall, especially as he had been a faithful servant of the department for a number of years. This removal left him practically without any means of support, and at a time when business was stagnant and he could not get employment of any kind; and he has not a position of any kind to-day. In my judgment, the fairest thing would have been to allow Humphries to retain the position of caretaker. The ^Government had recognized the merits of Mr. Humphries. They had considered him a valuable official, and he should have been treated decently at all events, and allowed to retain this particular position at $65 a month. He had started in as caretaker of the Immigration hall and had always held that position while he was gradually being promoted to more responsible positions.

The item under discussion is No. 64, which is to provide $620,000 for the salaries of agents and employees of Canada, Great Britain and foreign countries. That is an increase of $20,000 over last year's vote. Now if Mr. Humphries was dismissed or retired from his position on the grounds of economy, perhaps the minister would be good enough to explain this increase in the vote?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Of course, this is an estimate for next year. As the hon. gentleman realizes, there was practically no boundary inspection at all up to 1908. Two classes of people seek to come into Canada: first, desirable settlers, whom we are anxious to get; and, secondly, undesirable settlers, whom we are trying to keep out. The development of the boundary inspection accounts for no small proportion of the gradual increase in the expenditure of the Immigration Department. In practically every province there are railways connecting with the United States, and undesirables could easily slip in if a close watch were not kept. In 1909, the first year we had boundary inspection at all, 37 were appointed; in 1911, prior to the old Government going out of power, there were 87; that is, they had increased the number

of inspectors by 50 within two years. In February, 1915, there were 152 inspectors. This increase in the boundary inspection, together with increases in salaries that might take place, largely accounts for the extra $20,000. Although we are asking for $620,000, it does not necessarily follow that we shall spend all of that amount; but we are very anxious to guard the international boundary at this time. While we do not expect a large increase of overseas immigration, undesirables from the United States, which is going through a time of stress just like Canada, will 'Seek .new pastures and endeavour to get into Canada. They have been trying it already, and every year the immigration laws in that respect have to be enforced more strictly.
What salary does an inspector get?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: He starts at $900, and gradually increases to $1,200.
