The minister's explanation makes Humphries' case very much worse, because Humphries was a boundary inspector, and an especially good one; so that according to the minister's statement there was absolutely no reason to cut down expenses in regard to Mr. Humphries. Lethbridge is an important point of access from across the boundary, and it has always been necessary and always will be necessary to have a capable man there to watch for undesirables. That being the case and in view of the_ hon. minister's admission that he finds it necessary to increase the strength of his boundary staff, his defence of the removal of Humphries clearly falls to the ground, and we must accept the other alternative that Humphries was removed because of political pressure.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: He was a travelling inspector.
But his business as an inspector was rather to keep people out than to bring people in, that is why he was there, and that is what he was particularly efficient at.
What is the difference between a travelling inspector and a stationary inspector?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: A travelling inspector has jurisdiction over several points, while a stationary inspector has jurisdiction over only one.
One might be a Grit and the other a Tory.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: And one might be a Tory and the other a Grit.

I do not want this discussion to be confined entirely to western members. Being a resident of the city of Montreal, and knowing the conditions that prevail there now, and the fact that probably three-fourths of the unemployed there are not native Canadians, I would ask the minister if there is going to be any change in our immigration policy during the continuance of the present crisis, or whether anybody is to be allowed to come into this country just as usual.
The country districts can get along very well, but cities like the port of Montreal, into which foreigners come to seek labour, have to look after the needs of a great number of these people. The corporation of the city of Montreal is spending this winter close on $70,000 in charity; and the Archbishop of Montreal has written to me to say that they have organized 75 sections of the St. Vincent de Paul Society to cover the city, and were providing at present for nearly 20,000 people. The Grey Nuns and other charitable institutions in Montreal are supplying 2,000 quarts of soup daily, and Montreal is at present going through the most severe crisis in the memory of those living. Is the minister taking any means to prevent Montreal being flooded by foreigners without any means of livelihood?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There has been practically no immigration from across the sea since the war started; it has cured itself. The Government are not encouraging people to come here, and we are practically not making any active propaganda even in the British Isles. We are more strictly enforcing the immigration regulations than at any time in the past. We are not encouraging any persons to come here except those belonging to the agricultural classes, and we are not paying any bonus on any of the labouring classes. We are even getting more strict in regard to domestic servants. In some places there is yet a little demand for domestic servants, but in other places the supply is probably greater than the demand. Formerly, some came over as domestic servants who were not really domestic servants before leaving their own country, and now they must prove, to the satisfaction of the officers, that they have been in domestic service at least twelve months prior to sailing. There are some who come to the country of their own volition.
Some are encouraged by railway companies.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That may be, but they have to comply with the immigration regulations and pass the medical examination.
If mechanics or labourers come here how are they allowed in?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have an order prohibiting them from entering British Columbia, and while we are not directly prohibiting mechanics from coming in to other parts, yet our agents on the other side have been instructed to discourage them in every possible way.

The return with regard to the Civil Service shows that up to March 4, 1914, 110 officials of the Immigration Department were dismissed, 35 resignations received, and 343 appointed in their places. The minister has explained that there has been an increase in the boundary immigration agents of 50; will he say whether the remainder of the increase was in the inside service or the outside service?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We have had some increases in the inside service as well as in the outside service. We have opened two new offices in the United States, in England we have opened offices at Carlisle, Peterborough and Cardiff, and one in Copenhagen, all of which require staffs.
Mr. W. M. MARTIN': The new officers would be included in the figures given last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
The return is brought down to March 4, 1914, over a year ago; can the minister say how the Immigration Department stands to-day, as regards the number of its officials?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There have been very few increases since that return was brought down.
I presume the officials employed in the drought-stricken districts in the West would come under the Immigration Department and would contribute to the increase?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: These are teihporary employees for a few months.
How many are employed in the drought-stricken area distributing relief as temporary officials?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are about fourteen each in Maple Creek district, north and south, and about twenty in the Moosejaw district.

And apart from these
there have been few appointed to the Immigration Department since the date of that return?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

The cost of administering the department has increased very largely since 1911. What is the justification for that? The total cost of the Immigration Department, 1911-12, was $1,364,999; in 1913-.14, $1,893,297, and for the current year, 1914-15, $2,138,800 or an increase of 65 per cent over 1911-12. The increase in 1913-14 over 1911-12 is about $530,000, and the increase in 1914-15 over 1913-14 is about $300,000. This I cannot understand. In 1911-12 and 1913-14, immigration into this country was about as high as in any year of our history, but in 1914 the immigration has been very light. The minister, I suppose, will answer that since August 4, 1914, when war was declared, it would not be fair to make a comparison, but for the first eight months of 1914 the immigration had dropped off immensely. The immigration for 1911-12 amounted to 354,257, and for 1913-14 to 168,859. The cost of each immigrant in 1912 was four dollars, and the cost of each immigrant in 1914 was twelve dollars. I realize that even though immigration is practically stopped the minister cannot dismiss the officials and disband the organization.
But there must be some reason for this tremendous increase in the expenditure. We are getting no better service; we are getting no better immigrants than we were getting before. The minister might give the committee some explanation why the cost has increased so largely.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
rather confusing the fiscal year in one instance with the calendar year in another. He just took the year 1914 as a calendar year.

That is in regard to the number of immigrants. I compared fiscal years when I was speaking of the cost. The minister says it cost $12 per capita for immigration in 1914. I could not tell, of course, what the number of immigrants were for the last three months of 1914-15.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The cost per capita for the fiscal year, 1913-14, amounted to $3.80. The cost per capita of immigration in a time of financial stringency is always greater than it is in a time of prosperity. No better illustration of that is required than in the year 1908. For that year the cost per capita of immigration ran up several dollars during the time of financial stress. Then, of course, my hon. friend is comparing the Estimates of the past year, that is 1914-15, with what was expended in 1912. We are not expending all our Estimates for 1914-15. We expect that out of our vote for the current year we shall have left unexpended at the end of the fiscal year some $300,000. The Estimates might be cut and slashed, but it does not do not to have sufficient funds on hand in a department which is engaged in handling human beings. No better illustration of that is necessary than that during the present year, as the hon. member will know, in a portion of our country in Saskatchewan and Alberta, that is the drought-stricken area, the people were left almost absolutely destitute. They required prompt attention. We had no particular appropriation for that purpose, but we used the immigration vote. We advanced out of that vote $120,000 for the relief of those settlers. Our immigration and our homesteads are so intimately associated that we thought we were justified in doing so. Our immigration until this past year has been keeping very well. During 1913-14, the last fiscal year, we had the largest immigration that we have had in the history of our country, save one year, namely, the preceding year. The immigration in 1912-13-was 402,000, and in 1013-14, in round numbers, 385,000, a drop of some 17,000. Since the war started, we have had absolutely no overseas immigration at all. If the war continues, I do not expect we shall expend all the money we are appropriating this year, but I think we ought to take the precaution of having the money on hand. Supposing the war should cease in July or August, we might have a large influx of people into this country, and we desire to have the money to cope with the situation. The fact that we have the money there does not mean that we are going to spend it all.

There has been a large
falling off in immigration from Europe.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

The fact, of course, is attributable to the war, but what is the rea 994
son for the decline in immigration from the United States?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I might offer one explanation. About two years ago the United States opened up a large area of new territory. The lands, of course, are inferior, and the men are given what is known as enlarged homesteads of 320 acres, to enter into competition with our homestead entries and pre-emptions. That undoubtedly has had some effect. Some professional homesteaders may have come to our country and secured patents and then gone back to the United States to take up 320 acres there, or Canadians may have gone to the United States to take up 320 acres. The United States authorities have tried to put a stop to that by making the time on the land seven months in order to prevent a man from homesteading in both Canada and the United States.

Is there a homesteading
repatriation movement in certain districts?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
What measure of success has been obtained?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There has been some
measure of success, especially from the United States.
Can the minister give me the extent of the repatriation from the United States during the past few months?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In the last twelve months I understand that about 55,000 have come from the United States, and perhaps 20 per cent of those would be French Canadians repatriated.
Have they gone West?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
A good portion of them
have gone West. Some of them have settled along the National Transcontinental line.
I was informed some time ago that the department had appointed Mr. Peter Webb as general immigration agent for some particular portion of Nova Scotia. Is that a fact?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

Has an application
been received from Mr. Webb for the position?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not to my knowledge. The hon. gentleman was not in the House before 6 o'clock?
No.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This question was asked
by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair).
I am asking for information for myself.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There was a petition sent in asking for his appointment.

Has the minister
seconded the efforts of Rev. Mr. Caron, who has been endeavouring to bring in settlers along the National Transcontinental railway from C-oohrane east towards the city of Quebec ? Last year I gave some figures in the House. Rev. Mr. Caron had 300 settlers on one excursion.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Is he not employed by the Provincial Government ?
I think he had some mission from the Dominion Government. He is probably employed by the province. His literature was printed, I think, under the auspices of the department.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: He may be associated with one of the colonization societies.
Has the minister any information ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not 'here.

A complaint was made at the time that the National Transcontinental was not being operated, and that those settlers were taken in under very great difficulties. The letter I received at the time said that a group of them who were ready to leave their homes in Quebec had to go by a round-about route through Ontario and then come back to Quebec. That is too large a question, however, to take up to-night. I do not know whether any arrangement has been made since then by the department to facilitate settlement along the line of the National Transcontinental from Quebec westward.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand several of the colonization agents are using their best endeavours to get settlers along the National 4 Transcontinental. I do not know about this particular district.
The department is not doing anything itself ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.
Does the minister not think it should do something ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
When I say no, the department is1 paying some of the colonization agents. I do not know whether this [Mi-. Chisholm.]
gentleman is paid by the department or not. Several of those colonization agents are in the employ of the Government and they are bringing in settlers along the line of the National Transcontinental.

Outside of paying the
salaries of the agents, does the department give any assistance to the work?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No, except by grants to
colonization societies.
They have the distribution of the funds?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

I think I understood the minister to say two or three minutes ago that no effort is being put forward to bring labouring men into the country at the present time, and I also understood him to say that efforts are being put forward to bring in men to put on the land.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We are not paying bonuses on any class of immigrants coming to Canada except agriculturists, agricultural labourers and domestic servants. Those are the only classes of people whom we are encouraging to come into the country.
Is the minister paying people to come to this country?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is a bonus paid to
booking agents for every agriculturist they bring into the country. We do not pay passages, and we do not assist the immigrants themselves in any way.
Do you make it a condition that immigrants shall settle in the country districts and not in the cities?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We endeavour to do so.
We have immigration agents to look after them.

The minister realizes
the importance of having them settle on the land?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

The decision of
the minister as to the present condition of affairs is a very wise one. I agree that we should bring into the country at the present time only agriculturists-men who will go on to the land. For the future policy of immigration into this country, that would be the very best policy that the minister could adopt, and it would be in the bestt interests of the country. We have in this country too many men who do not go on to the land. If you take the

figures for the last few years and compare the population of the various cities with the population of the country, districts, you will be surprised to find how much, faster the population in the cities has increased than the population of the rural parts of the country has done. I find that from 1900 to 1910 the rural population of the whole of Canada increased only 574,000, whereas the city population in the same time increased by 1,250,000, or 2J times as fast as the rural population did. A portion of that increase in the cities must be due to the fact that we in Canada have not pursued the right policy of bringing immigration into this country. We * have pursued the policy of getting men in in numbers, and not of picking the men whom we allow to come in. We all agree that we should build up the agricultural districts from one end of the country to the other. The cities apparently grow fast enough of themselves. Out of all the immigrants who came into the country during the last fifteen years, a large percentage went into the cities. It is difficult to understand why they go there. A large number of people go on to the land as farm labourers and homesteaders for a short time, and then gradually drift into the cities, and they do so under conditions that lead to starvation amongst a great many of them. I have never been able to understand why it is that people in this country will drift into the cities. They must be attracted by the glamour and pleasures of the cities. Wages may have something to do with it. It is generally understood that the wages paid in our cities are higher than the wages paid on the farms; but very often a man on a farm gets his board and lodging in addition to his wages. In that case the wages on the farm a*e almost as good as the wages paid in the cities. As a matter of fact, if you take the total amount of wages paid every year in the great manufacturing cities of Canada, and the total number of men who work in those factories, and find the average, it runs from $35 to $39 per month. Therefore, in so far as wages are concerned, there is simply no reason why men should drift into the cities from the farms. There are great industries in Canada. One is the manufacturing industry, and another is the agricultural industry. In so far as the strength of the industries are concerned, the agricultural industry at the present time is far ahead of the manufacturing industry, not only in the amount of capital invested, but in the amount of men employed and in the amount of production.
I think there is no question that our great success in the future will depend upon whether we have or have not a successful body of farmers and proper conditions surrounding those farmers. It is the duty not only of the Dominion Government but of the Provincial Government and of our municipal institutions to attempt to make conditions on the farm more pleasing to the people and thereby increase the production' of our farms. If the Department of Immigration should not attempt to bring in any but agriculturists it would be well advised and its policy would be in the interests of the country.

We took evidence for two years upon this very question before the Old Age Pensions Committee. We had people there from all over Canada, people in every walk of life. They were sworn and they gave their evidence absolutely without prejudice. I think that if the hon. gentleman will peruse that testimony he will find out largely why it is that the times seem so out of joint. It is true, there is a degree of glamour about life in the city-not in Montreal, I should judge by what is stated by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil)-
In Peterborough.

-but people like to be together where they can enjoy the moving picture shows, the advantages of the churches, the schools, and so on. But the fact of the matter is that life in the country -so the testimony shows-is such a disjointed, unorganized, unreliable sort of affair that the people do not really know what to make of it. The consequence is that when an attempt is made to move from the city to the country the people find they are up against hostile conditions. There is a chilly reception on the part of the people of the country for the urban settler. A man is easily swallowed up when he goes into the city from the country, but it is very hard for him to be swallowed up when he goes from the city to the country. The upshot of it all undoubtedly will be that strenuous conditions such as are spoken of by the hon. member for Bonaventure as existing in Montreal will compel the Government to devise some means of distributing the population of the country with advantage to themselves and advantage to the state. To my mind it is an absolutely senseless proposition to keep on asking people to come in here from outside *[DOT]men we are making no attempt tr>
ogen

erate conditions at home. I cannot understand-no doubt, it is largely due to my limited understanding-why we should allow these conditions to continue. This country shows the extraordinary condition of tens of thousands of people in the bread line, roaming you may say through the purlieus of the cities in quest of work or food, and in a terrible condition of both body and mind and with no prospect for the future. These conditions, of course, may be said to have been brought about by fifteen years of misrule. They are not the product of a day, all must admit that.
As one of those who sat on the Old Age Pensions Committee, I deem it my duty to express the opinion that something ought to be done; that it is entirely improper to ignore the conditions revealed by the evidence taken before that committee at considerable expense. I must protest against any attempt to bring people in from outside until such time as we reconstruct the conditions within our country. Perhaps it is due to the fact that a momentous war is taking place, but conditions are rapidly becoming very serious in Canada. I do not think we are humane; I do not think we display that loving kindness which we certainly ought to display. Economic considerations are our daily care, but solicitude for the people is not; we are prepared to let them go to the block. I wish in my humble way to call attention to this fact. The situation must be dealt with; the people cannot and must not be ignored. This movement from the city to the country must be carried on with some degree of skill and promptitude. The continuance of the present system of calling people from all over the world to come to our country, at considerable expense to ourselves, while at the same time not extending a brass farthing for the benefit of our own people in that respect, is something that is quite beyond me.
Is any provision likely to be made for the inspection of immigrants when they take passage on the other side instead of when they reach this country?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I presume the hon. mem' her means by that: have we duplicated our medical inspection system, or have we under consideration the idea of abolishing our Canadian inspection and adopting in lieu thereof inspection on the other side of the ocean. As to the latter, we have not done so. As to the former, any persons who attempt to come into Canada in contraven-

tion of our immigration regulations or who prove to be undesirable, are within a certain specified time taken back to their homes at the expense of the steamship companies, and the onus is upon the steamship' companies to see that they do not bring over any undesirables. They have medical inspection on the other side of the ocean. The inspectors examine the emigrants before they board ships, and accompany the vessel on the trip over. In addition to that, the boards of trade in the old country have their system of medical examination. If we attempted to put a staff of medical men over there, I do not think they would have any real status, and in respect of cases developing on board ship, we would still have to have a staff in Canada as well. I admire the hon. gentleman's persistency in trying to bring about the adoption of his suggestion in this regard. Theoretically, his doctrine is all right; I approved it more or less myself when in opposition. But when you have the responsibilities of administration on your shoulders, you have to take other things into consideration. It must be agreed that the carrying out of this principle is surrounded by a great many difficulties. In the (first place, when the emigrants get on board ship at Glasgow, Liverpool and other parts, they arrive but a short time before the departure of the ships, and any medical inspection made at that time would necessarily be a very hurried one. There are features connected with deportation which we all deplore; families are broken up, persons in this country are unable to bring their friends over. But before these people take passage for Canada they know what regulations they have to comply with, financially and otherwise. More persons are rejected by reason of their not measuring up to the financial requirements than for any other reason; nevertheless, they all know before they leave their own country what the requirements are in this respect.

The hon. minister
is perhaps not aware, as some of us in the East are, that families that land in New York or at our own ports are often broken up for some reason; the mother or the child has to return to the other side. Expense should not stand in the way of adjustment of this matter. If the people are not fit to come into the country, they are not fit to come when the ship leaves the other side. Of course, in some cases, objections may develop on the way over, but as a general rule every person coming to this country

should know before he leaves the other side whether he will be allowed to land here or not. My hon. friend says that the great trouble is shortage of dollars and cents. I do not think it is a good policy to reject persons for that reason; many men possessing but $5 may be much more desirable than others who have as much as $200. For the past six sessions I have urged this matter upon the department, pointing out that it is an injustice and a crime that families who are brought out to this country simply because some immigration agent makes a little out of it. should be broken up when they get to this side. Once more- probably it is the last opportunity I shall ever have to do so in the House-I wish to impress upon the minister the necessity of inspecting emigrants on the other side instead of when they reach Canada.
How many officials were added to the immigration staff at Winnipeg between September 1 and December 31, 1914?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I would have to get that
information for the hon. member. Very few additions to the staff have been made; those who have been added to the staff have been placed there temporarily in connection with seed grain distribution.
Has the minister a representative of his department in Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I believe we have one in Charlottetown.
Can the minister give me his name?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. McCready. He has been located at. Charlottetown.
He is called publicity agent. How many men are employed in a similar capacity in Nova Scotia?	_

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: One.

After calling the attention of the minister to the conditions existing in Montreal and to the importance of controlling the immigration into that city, I procured from my room the letter addressed to me on the 15th of March by the secretary of the St. Vincent de Paul Society of Montreal. It is well known that the English, Irish and Scotch societies look after the poor of their own nationalities and the St. Vincent de Paul Society covers the French Canadian population,
which of course forms the great bulk of the population of Montreal. Mr. Venier says that last year they came to the relief of three times as many poor people as in former years, and that they have been obliged to organize 75 sections of the society to cover the island of Montreal. On the 15th of February the officers of the society were visiting 3,524 families consisting of 7,094 adults and 11,476 children, forming a total of 18,570 who were receiving charity at that time from this society alone. Many of these are of course Canadians, but a large number are not Canadians, but people who have come to this country, who have gone into employment in the country districts and gradually worked their way into the city. Many of them are of foreign extraction and have become a charge on the community. The society, up to February 21 of this year had expended $54,690 in charity. It must be said to the credit of this society that not one dollar of this money has been paid for services of any of its officials, all the work done by members of the society is done purely for charity. No man or woman receives one dollar for his or her services and therefore this $54,690 is the amount actually expended for charity up to that time. He goes on to say that in the months of January and February alone 137,399 free soups were given to applicants by the charitable institutions in Montreal. This letter is in French, otherwise I would have read it for the benefit of the minister; but I would like to impress upon him the importance, as long as the present conditions exist in Europe and are reflected in Canada, of having very stringent measures adopted by the department to prevent the coming to this country of any man, woman or child liable to become a charge on our cities, because when the country districts are unable to look after these people they work into the cities. Montreal, at the present time, looks after the sick, the maimed, the wounded, the unemployed of practically all of the province of Quebec and a portion of eastern Ontario. When they have no relief of any kind in any of the smaller municipalities or villages, if they are sick beyond the assistance that can be given to them in the rural districts, they work into the cities and the cities have to look after them. The work of this society is greatly to its credit. I wish to impress on the minister the necessity of stringent measures on the opening of navigation to see that no person comes to this

country who is likely to become a charge upon it. This is the most important subject that the Administration has to face in the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If the Iron, gentleman had inquired a little more closely he would have found that the great bulk of these people are not immigrants.
I said that.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: I notice there is a considerable reduction in this vote.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We are economizingcutting down in our advertising and other expenses. We are not expending as much on literature as we did. The High Commissioner is supervising our expenses in

the Old Country in conjunction with the assistant superintendent, Air. Smith, and has recommended that certain items of expenditure be omitted during the present year.
Will there be a reduction in the number or the character of the atlases that have usually been issued by the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is something we have a considerable demand for. We issue just enough to supply the demands of our agents in the United States and Great Britain.

I believe there are two
atlases issued; one an atlas of Canada, and the other a western atlas. Can the minister say what the average yearly cost of these atlases has been for the last few years?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I can not give the exact
figures just now, but the price has remained about the same for several years.
Where are they printed?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The Alontreal Gazette
prints a large number of them. The atlases for United States distribution are printed in Chicago, by Rand, AIcNally & Co., I think.
Air. OLI\TER. Which atlas does the Gazette print?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The atlas of Canada.
Immigration-administration of Chinese immigration ; salaries, $30,000 ; contingencies, $20,000.
Would the minister make a statement as to how our Chinese immigration during the last fiscal or calendar year compares with the previous years?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In 1913-14 there were 238
exempts, and in (the nine months of 1014-15 only 95. In 1913-14, 5,274 paid the head tax, and for the nine months of 1914-15, 1,148. The total revenue for 1913-14 was $2,644,593, for the nine months of 1914-15, $577,912. There has been no Chinese immigration since the first of July, for it is prohibited by the Order in Council passed last year.
Do you keep track of the Chinese after they come into Canada?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The American authorities
say that we get the head tax, and they get the Chinamen.
There is a large colony of Chinamen in Alontreal. Has the department no control over them?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

Perhaps the rule works
the other way, and we may be getting the Chinese, whether the United States gets the head tax or not. There is no doubt at all that there is a very large Chinese population in Canada, and that it is increasing. Would the minister say whether it is the policy of the Government to permit or restrict the further increase of that population.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Order in Council prohibits them from coming into Canada at all, which is about the best form of restriction we can have. According to the last census there were about 27,000 Chinese in Canada. Since 1885, 87,000 have come into Canada.

The prohibition of the
entry of Chinese applies only to British Columbia courts?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
That is practically the
only way they come in.

It may be the only way
they come in legally, but I am not at all satisfied that it is the only way they do come in. I think they have the same advantage in crossing the United States boundary as other people have.

Three is no Japanese or
Hindu immigration at the present time?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No Hindu, and very little Japanese.
Are the Japanese subject to the same restrictions as the Chinese?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Under the Lemieux agreement with Japan me immigration cannot exceed a certain number.

Not even in war time
when they are our Allies?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The immigration does not reach the limit stipulated in the agreement.
The Order in Council does not apply to them?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

The minister has stated
that there were so many exempts. On what condition do they become exempt?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Tnose who are exempt are merchants and their families, and students who come to attend Canadian colleges or schools. It has been strongly urged that we should make our regulations more generous in regard to the admission of Chinese students. It is claimed that the Un.instates are very much more liberal in that respect, and thait they derive an advantage commercially for when these students go home after completing their course they practically become commercial agents and advertise the Unitea States quite extensively.

The reas n I ask about
exempts is that before I left Edmonton a gentleman called on me and made representations in regard to the right of a naturalized Chinaman to bring over his wife from China. This man was able to pay the head tax, but did not wish to pay it. He did not consider it compatible with the dignity of a Canadian citizen. That is as it nas been represented to me. Might I ask whether in such a case -ie woman would, be exempt from the head tax?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
If this gentleman was a
merchant his wife would be exempt, but if he was not a merchant the fact of his being naturalized would not allow his wife to escape the head tax.

That is as it was represented to me. Half a dozen Chinamen may come to Canada ana be constituted a mercantile company, and then they are entitled to bring in their wives free. This particular Chinaman came in many years ago, I believe as an employee, and though not a merchant he runs a large laundry ana employs a considerable quantity of labour.
He is debarred from the privilege that is accorded others under circumstances that would seem not to entitle them to it so much as he. I am not making any plea on his behalf; I am merely placing before the minister the case as I received it. Under the circumstances I have stated, does the prohibition still stand?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, unless he is a merchant. If we were to allow every one who runs a laundry to come in with his family, without paying the head-tax, there would be difficulty.

There are two timber reserves near Dauphin, one called the Riding Mountain reserve and the other called the Duck Mountain reserve, and it is rumoured through the country that these reserves are always held up as plums before the people at election time. It has even been said that men who vote right in the elections are promised homesteads on these reserves. What is the policy of the minister with respect to the further opening up of

these timber reserves; are there going to be any more homesteads on them or will they be left as they are?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is not my intention to interfere at all with the boundaries of either the Riding mountain or the Duck mountain. Where any lands are withdrawn it is by reason of an inspection made and a report .to the minister, and they are taken out by Act of Parliament. It is not my intention to withdraw any lands from the existing boundaries.
Then the position would be that there would not be any more homesteads there?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There will not be any more homesteads.

I am afraid the statement of the minister will cause some consternation among his political supporters in that district. At the last local election in Manitoba, and even in the election before, it was stated that those who voted Conservative were to get homesteads on one of these reserves. I moved for the papers some time ago, but I suppose they will not be brought down now so late in the session.
I have asked if there was an investigation conducted by Inspector Cuttle, into certain things that took place in connection with the Duck Mountain reserve. Does the minister know anything about it?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I know of no investigation conducted by Inspector Cuttle regarding any lands in connection with the Duck Mountain reserve.

The source of my information is reliable and I can well understand that there might be an investigation which the minister would know nothing about, on account of the extent of his department. Ihe facts brought to my notice are briefly these: it is said that the investigation was held either at a place called Roblin or As-sessippi, into certain charges of irregularities in the opening up of the timber on the Duck Mountain reserve. At that investigation there were five different witnesses, whose names I have here, who appeared and said they were to get the privilege of squatting on certain tracts of land on that reserve and subsequently to get the right of homesteading, if they voted Conservative in the provincial election. The second condition imposed on them was, that they should pay $100 each to a man named R. H. Keay, who is a justice of the peace, and 
magistrate at a place called Roblin. I am also informed that there was evidence given before Mr. Cuttle at that investigation, that no fewer than 17 promissory notes for $100 each were drawn up in a certain store in, I think, Roblin, and signed by 17 of these applicants for homesteads, and that all of these men subsequently were allowed homestead entries. I do not pay very much attention to the fact that they voted Conservative, but I do pay attention, if what I am told is true, to the fact that 17 men had paid $100 each to a justice of the peace located in that part of the country, as a condition precedent to their getting a homestead. If that is the condition of affairs, I submit to the minister that it is very serious. I respectfully submit to the minister also, that if there has been no investigation and if these facts have not been brought to his attention previously, some investigation ought to take place now, and if what I am informed is true, some action should be taken.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Is Mr. Keay in the employ of this Government?
No. He is a justice of the peace and a very prominent Conservative in that district.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
What has he got to do
with it ?

Apparently he had everything to do with it, because fee had to get $100 before a man could get a homestead, and the most peculiar part of the affair is that the inspector who made the homestead report, subsequently, Inspector Spears, recommended every one of the men who paid the hundred dollars to get a homestead, and not a single man who did not pay one hundred dollars, got a homestead. I bring these facts to the attention of the minister in the hope that an investigation will be made. I know that the minister himself would not stand for it for a minute, but the minister is not aware-to use an expression I have heard used before-of all the skulduggery that goes on in Western Canada under the guise of his department. The minister does not know anything about it, and if he did he would not stand for it for a minute. I think the minister told us that there was no politics in his department in the West. As far as the Department of Immigration is concerned, I do not know whether they have politics in it or not.
I am not worrying about that veTy much, but I can tell the minister that there are

politics in the administration of the Department of the Interior, and whether he is >to blame for it ot not I do not know. A condition precedent to a man becoming homestead inspector in Saskatchewan is that he must be one of the most violent Tories in the district he resides in. There is not one of them who was not a violent Tory politician, and there is not one of them whom I know at the present time who is not more an election agent than he is a homestead inspector, and that not only in Dominion elections but in provincial elections. These are facts that should be brought to the attention of the minister because I know that so far as he is concerned he does not want to administer his department in a political way.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Whoever the hon. gentleman's informant is has informed him wrongly. The only lands I know of, taken out of the Duck Mountain reserve, were taken out prior to this Government coming into power and were given to so-called squatters, and the gentleman who did this subsequently on oath swore that be gave them to men who were friends of the then Administration, and who were not squatters at all. He did it by the wholesale, and he admitted he did it. That is all I know about the Duck Mountain reserve. As to the questions which the hon. gentleman has been putting on the Order Paper as lto Inspector Cuttle's investigation into the Duck Mountain reserve, he has been truthfully answered. Inspector Cuttle held no investigation respecting any land regarding Duck mountain.
I did not put any question on the Order Paper about Duck mountain; I moved for the papers.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: When was that investigation held?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: After the New Year.
Was it not in December or last fall?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Instructions may have been given to hold the investigation in December, but I do not think the investigation was held until after the New Year. The man stated that because he' was a Liberal, he was denied a homestead, whereas other settlers who had signed notes to a man- he did not say who the man was-had been allowed to take up homesteads. It chanced that the assizes were going on in my own town, and a Mr. Keay, who was on the Grand Jury, came to see me at my residence.	In discussing matters
generally, I	told him	of this
complaint that had been forwarded to me by the department. I immediately replied to the department: " That kind of thing

cannot go on, if it is going on, and I wish you to authorize an investigation to be held to see if those charges are true." I mentioned this matter to Mr. Keay. Mr. Keay said: "Oh, there is nothing in it; I am the individual to whom they refer. What happened was this: In a few instances those Galicians who had squatted upon the land did not know where their stakes were, because the grass and scrub had grown up and covered them. I am old settler there "-he lives at Assessippi ;- "they asked me if I would go out and locate their lines. I went out. I charged them a fee for doing so. I got very little, but I took some notes." He left the wrong impression upon my mind. He left the impression that there were only two or three cases and that it was a matter of only $10 or $15. Therefore I ordered Mr. Cuttle to hold the investigation. Mr. Cuttle went up there; held the investigation; took the evidence under oath, and found that Mr. Keay had taken about seventeen notes for $100 a-piece from those people for locating them upon the land, not because they had voted this way or that, because as a matter of fact the evidence does not show that. I have read the evidence.
The information that I received came from a man who gave evidence before Mr. Cuttle.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Was that Mr. McLellan?

I do not wish to give the name to the minister. I am informed that this man gave evidence before Mr. Cuttle to the effect that he saw seventeen of those notes made out for $100 a-piece in favour of Mr. Keay, and that five of the men themselves said that they had to give the notes before they could get homesteads. If the report shows anything else, the evidence was not reported correctly.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not think that is in the evidence of Mr. McLellan. He swore that it was a very ordinary thing for these Ruthenians to offer money to the Canadian settlers to do this kind of work. In fact, he said, he had been offered it many times himself, and they look upon it as nothing wrong. He entirely exonerated the officials of the department of wrong-doing. This man Keay had nothing to do with the department. He went out to locate the land. These notes were given, but I wrote to the homestead inspector and the inspector of land agencies to notify each and

every one of the men who had given the notes not to to pay a dollar. I said it was nothing less than robbery. I told him he would not take it into court if he has any regard for his reputation. I may say that I am no longer a friend of Keay's if that is any satisfaction to the hon. gentleman.

He is a justice of the
peace.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We do not appoint justices of the peace.
That is highly to the minister's credit.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
He imposed upon these settlers, no doubt. I do not know that the evidence shows that in any case these notes had been paid, though it shows that the notes were given. I gave instructions that they were not to be paid. Nobody connected with the department had anything to do with it. There was no promise about votes; it "was after the Provincial elections had been held. These people did not know they were going to have their rights protected until the month of October. That was the month I returned from Rochester, and I was glad to know that no appointee of this department had anything to do with it, and I think Mr. McLellan was good enough to state that in his evidence.
Government of the Yukon Territory-salaries and expenses conected with the administration of the Territory, $128,000.
Will the minister give us an idea of the population of the Yukon at this time?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
If hon. members do not
mind, I will ask the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Alfred Thompson) to speak, as he is better posted on the subjeot than I.
The population of the Yukon at the last census enumeration was about 9,000.

In what year was that
taken?

In 1911. The population of the Yukon fluctuates somewhat. Last year a few more people came into the Territory than left it.
The Yukon-grant to local council, $125,000.
How is that expended?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We make a grant and the local council expends it.
What is it expended for?

In building roads and trails in outlying districts, repairing bridges and maintaining roads already built; also in providing for hospitals and schools and for other charges devolving upon the local government of the territory. Besides this we have a special grant this year of $100,000 for roads. Nothing is a more important factor in the development of a frontier country than transportation. This is particularly true of the Yukon, where the cost of freighting goods and supplies from the coast cities or from the East to the Territory is exceedingly high, compared with charges in other sections of Cahada. These moneys are used chiefly for transportation purposes.

Does mining remain the
chief industry of the Territory?

Yes, and I am glad
to inform the committee that the output of gold has been well maintained for the last few years. We are producing about $5,000,000 per year in gold. We have also some very encouraging prospects in the way of silver-lead mines in a new section of the territory recently opened on the Upper Stewart river. Copper mining has been successfully carried on at White Horse in the southern end of the territory, and was in a very promising state until the outbreak of the war, when the prices	of	metals dropped	and
mining had to be temporarily suspended. Coal mining is also a factor in the economic development of the Territory, and geologists tell us that we have within the four corners of the Yukon five billion tons of good coal.
Of what kind?
It belongs to the lignite series so far as yet discovered. It it fairly well distributed.
Is placer mining carried on?

There are three classes of placer mining, the original method of thawing hoist and sluice-box, the dredging method and the hydraulic method. The greater part of the gold is won by the use of huge dredges which float in their own ponds. The dredging industry in the Yukon is carried to a very high state of development; we have some of the very largest gold dredges in the world. These are driven by electricity developed from the water-powers on the Klondvke river itself.
Are there any American companies operating in the Yukon at present?

Yes, we have one large American company, one Canadian company, and another company is being floated which will be chiefly English capital. There is in the outlying districts of the Klondyke, and in fact in other districts of the Yukon, the ordinary placer mining concerning which the hon. member asked. But in the older creeks in the Klondyke district itself, gold is won chiefly by dredging and hydraulicking.
Has there been any improvement in the transportation facilities within the last year or two? Is the country easier of access?
Not so far as the building of railways is concerned. We still use the railway connecting tide-water at Skagway, Alaska, with Whitehorse, on the Yukon river.
This road runs in American territory?

Twenty-three miles
from tide-water to the summit is in Ameri

can territory. The road is 110 miles long. When we reach the Yukon river, the freight is transferred to river boats and carried down to Dawson. Of course, we have a system of boats going right to Behring sea. Freight can be transhipped there to ocean boats and taken down the North Pacific to the ports of British Columbia and Washington. There is a regular steamship service there.
How much royalty is collected on the $5,000,000 of gold output?
The royalty on gold in the Yukon is 21 per cent. Every dollar's worth of gold raised must pay this royalty at the Gold Commissioner's office.

What proportion of this
$5,000,000 was taken out by the more primitive method, aside from hydraulicking and dredging?

I could not give the figures exactly, but I should say that at least four and a half millions of that gold is won by dredging and hydraulicking. Certainly not more than three-quarters of a million is won by the ordinary placer mining method to-day.

Where is the gold
assayed?

A good deal of it is
shipped to our own assay office at the Mint in Ottawa. It is sent in small bricks byregistered mail direct to the mint. This was the rule until the beginning of 1914, but for a time the Mint was not in a position to handle our gold because they weie enlarging the refinery and so the refinery was not working. The gora that our own mint does not get, goes to the mint in California, in the main. Some goes to the Seattle assay office. When the Klondyke was discovered the United States placed an assay office in the city of Seattle for the purpose of getting the Klondyke and Alaskan gold to come to the Pacific coast cities. That was a very good, thing for them to do; their policy justified itself. It resulted in a stream of our gold pouring into the Pacific coast cities of the United States for years, and the cities of Seattle, Portland and San Francisco benefited very materially. At that time we were not in a position to handle our own output of gold. Since then, I am glad to say, we have established an assay office of our own in Vancouver, and the gold may be marketed there. But it can also be forwarded to the mint here by either express or mail. A good deal of it comes here, and mat which does not come here, goes in the main, to San Francisco or to the assay office in Seattle.
Is the Yukon self-supporting so far as agriculture is concerned?

Not as yet. But there are great agricultural possibilities in the Yukon. One of the difficulties we have there is in importing feed for our stock. In the Yukon hay sells at the same price per pound as oats the year round, and in the fifteen years during which I have been in the Territory, I have never known hay to be sold for less than four cents a pound or $80 a ton, and at this time of the year, in the spring, it is from $100 to $120 a ton.
Quite a luxury.

Yes, however, the
United States Government is carrying on some very interesting experiments in agriculture in the Yukon valley, in Alaska, just across the boundary. They have there a gentleman named Georgeson who is attending to some agricultural experiment stations that they have in the Yukon valley. He has succeeded in getting a type of alfalfa which matures in Siberia in about our latitude and in about the same environment that we have in the Yukon

He has succeeded in transplanting and growing successfully yellow-flowered alfalfa in the Yukon valley. I have this information from himself and it is accurate. He entertains the hope that eventually the Yukon valley will raise its own fodder.

Where can the seed of
that alfalfa be procured?

I cannot say just
where it can be procured, but if my hon. friend will write to Professor Georgeson at Sitka, Alaska, who is in charge of the agricultural stations of the United States Government there, he will be glad to give him any information on the subject.

The farmers of Nova
Scotia have repeatedly tried to raise alfalfa and, on account of the climate, I suppose, have failed to do so successfully. It is grown very successfully in the western states, especially on the foothills of the Cascades. If there is a grade of alfalfa that will grow in a colder climate, it should be generally known so that the people may have an opportunity of getting the seed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My impression is that they have succeeded in growing alfalfa successfully in the neighbourhood of Sussex, in Kings county, N.B.

We grow excellent
potatoes there. Barley and oats ripen there every year. Wheat has been known to ripen there, although it is not grown extensively. The cost of labour is so great in the Yukon that up to the present time agriculture has not been carried on to the extent of the great possibilities the country offers.
What is the length of the summer season there-what we might call the farming season?

Wild flowers bloom in the vicinity of Dawson about the same time that they do in Ottawa-about the last week in April. We have practically no spring; just a plunge from winter into summer. May, June and July are our three summer months. August is a fall month; it is quite cool in September.

I suppose frost come in
August?
We have a frost every year in July. That is one thing we have to look out for in raising some of the tenderer plants.

You grow
potatoes there, but you cannot use them, can
.MARCH 26, 1915
you ? They are very large and soft, are they not ?

We have a great many things to learn about vegetables. What my hon. friend says is more or less true. Hon. gentlemen must understand that this ground is frozen to bed-rock. We have a very light rainfall there, and on account [DOT]of continuous thawing caused by the warm sun of summer, moisture rises from the frozen ground in sufficient quantities to make things .grow. Potatoes grown in the rich loam of the river bottoms are wet and soggy, to a certain extent, but on the hillsides, where the loam is more mixed with sand, where there is not so much vegetable matter, and where the hillsides are well diained, we can grow a potato that is very dry and mealy; really a good tuber.
I understand that you are quite successful in raising certain kinds of vegetables ?
Yes. Cauliflower and celery thrive there. Radishes grow rapidly and are very good. We raise tons of tomatoes, but under glass.
Are most of the people in the Yukon of Canadian origin?
Yes, they are of Canadian origin, or have become citizens of Canada. In the early days the greater number of the citizens were foreigners, but to-day they are practically all Canadians.
Is there any hope that in the near future there will be sufficient development to attract a larger population ?

Hope springs eternal in the human breast-this is particularly so among the prospectors in these metalliferous regions. Every year a small army of prospectors roam around among the hills; we always expect that one of them will discover another Klondyke, although, unfortunately, that hope has not yet been fulfilled. Only a small percentage of that vast territory of 200,000 square miles has yet been even examined in anything more than a most superficial way. The people live chiefly along the great water-courses, the Yukon and its tributaries. The country has a great future; the last page of its history has not yet been written by any means.
Relatively speaking, is ths country as good as Alaska is?

We believe it is, with this exception: we have not quite the
variety of climate that they have in Alaska. In the Yukon we are shut, off from the sea. The strip of sea-coast from Mount, St. Elias to the Portland canal went with the sale of Alaska to the United States by Russia; therefore we in the Yukon have no seacoast, on the Pacific, while the Alaskan people have. On that sea-coast they have a different climate altogether from what we have in the plateau which is drained by the Yukon river. So far as the interior of Alaska is concerned, perhaps our Yukon country is a little better, because we have in the south-eastern portion of the Yukon very large areas suitable for grazing, which eventually will be an important industry in the Yukon. As the Mackenzie River valley and the Northwest is settled, and grazing land becomes scarcer, the valleys of the rivers tributary to the Yukon will furnish grazers large areas where they can follow their business profitably.
Has there been any appreciable change in the climate of the Tukon within the last ten years, since the country has become more thickly populated?

I really think not. The records do not go back very far, but so far as they do give us information, we have not been able to notice that there has been any appreciable change. This winter has been exceptionally mild, but I think that mildness has prevailed all over the country.

When I was last in the Yukon I observed that fires had destroyed timber along the rivers. Is there a more systematic protection against fire now, and has there been any destruction of timber since that time? I would consider that such timber as there is there is very valuable, and that it is necessary to see that it is conserved at almost all costs.

The hon. member is right. Timber is a most valuable asset of our country, for its present and ruture development. We have lost a good deal of timber by fire, but we have fire rangers now whose particular business it is to stamp out fires.
The Northwest Mounted Police also do excellent work in this regard. We try to stamp fires out as soon as possible or prevent them if we can, because we realize how important it is to conserve our timber resources in that territory.

Grant to Local Council for maintenance of and repairs to roads, $100,000.
What are the principal roads?

The principal road is our winter road from Whitehorse, at the head of navigation on the Yukon to Dawson. -It is about 360 miles in length, and is our main thoroughfare for seven months in the year. Besides that we have roads radiating from Dawson to the gold-producing streams, a very fine system and one on which the Government has spent a great deal of money. The expenditure is justified because gold-mining is the basic industry of the country, and it is of the utmost importance to get supplies into the mines. This is in the immediate vicinity of Dawson, and we are extending the system up the Klondike valley and up the Stewart and White rivers. Wherever, in fact, there are indications of a camp being located, we try as soon as possible to give roads to connect with the watercourses,
How far does the winter road extend west from Whitehorse towards the Kluane valley?

We have a road there 150 miles through the interior towards the Kluane country, perhaps more. Then there are roads around Whitehorse, connecting the various mines with Whitehorse and some in Fortymile in the lower end of the territory. All of these roads cost a good deal of money to maintain from year to year and of course new roads are required from time to time. For instance, last year on the overland trail from Whitehorse to Dawson we put ferries on the Yukon and Stewart rivers, so that now a person may drive by automobile from the head of navigation to Dawson City.
The roads are fairly good?

Excellent roads, we
have automobiles and all kinds of carriages in this country.

Are the roads made with
gravel?

Yes, wherever we can, we build the roads on the side of the hills so that they are easily drained and have a gravel bottom. Of course, in crossing the tundra it is necessary to corduroy. The hon. member for Edmonton will bear me out that we have an excellent system of roads in that country considering that, it is a mining camp.

The hon. member says
that the road west of Whitehorse goes 150 miles. What is the communication from Whitehorse to the White river copper fields? Is there a wagon road all the way?
No.

How much is road and
how much is pack trail, or do they go in that tvay at all?

Yes, they go in that
way, that is the way they go in. In winter we have a trail connecting Whitehorse with the White River copper fields. In the summer they go by lake Kluane, which is 150 miles west of Whitehorse, and either hire or make boats there and sail down to the White river	and up the
White river to the	copper fields.
They may also go down the Yukon to the White river and up the White river ,to the copper fields. In the Estimates for the Public Works Department there is an item of $5,000 for the removal of obstructions to navigation in the Yukon. I intend to ask the Minister of Public Works to segregate $1,000 of that for the removal of some obstructions in the White river and the Donjek which connects Kluane lake with the White river. This will make it possible for boats to ply from the Yukon into lake Kluane and open up what is in itself a small empire. That will give the miners in that section, which is a promising section, excellent transport accommodation. This will enable them to cut their freight rates in two and you can understand the importance of what I say about transportation when I state that it costs from 14 to 20 cents a pound to get supplies into these remote mining camps. Anything we can do to assist the miner to get supplies to the seat of his operations aids to that extent in the development of that great territory.
Astronomical Surveys-investigations and demarcations of the exterior boundaries of Canada, the triangulation, levelling and topographic work of the Geodetic Survey of Canada, and astronomical work of the Department of the Interior, including the expenses of the Dominion Astronomical Observatory at Ottawa and the branch therefrom at Saanich Hill, B.C., and $1,000 to W. F. King, as International Boundary Commissioner, $260,000.

As this is a year of economy, I would ask the minister if the work demanded under this vote is so
11	p.m. urgent that it would not have been profitable to practise economy in regard to this particular vote?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is a good deal of
this which is uncompleted work. For instance, the boundary survey is made under treaty, and it must be done. We could not very well avoid it. It will not be very long before that is all completed. The portions yet uncompleted are the Ontario-Minnesota boundary and the Quebec-Maine boundary.
I think it would have been fairer if the vote had been divided between the boundary work and the geodetic survey. How much of this is for the geodetic survey?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
$125,000, and $60,000 for
the boundaries.
To provide for payments on account of the construction and installation of a large reflecting telescope for the Dominion Astronomical Observatory (Western Branch), $31,500.

What will be the total
cost of that telescope?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: A very little over $90,000.
What is the purpose to be achieved by the installation of this expensive instrument, that is as compared with the instruments previously in use?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This is a subject of a rather technical character and I do not profess to be familiar with the details. I understand that it will be the largest telescope in the world. We wished when installing a new telescope to have something that would be of the greatest credit to the country. A very large and influential deputation waited on us urging that this should be gone on with. Certain experiments were made to ascertain the most suitable place for its location, in Eastern and in Western Canada. It was decided that it would be far better at Saanich Hill, which is eight or nine miles out of Victoria. The road up to the telescope will be very expensive to build, but the Provincial Government are allowing us a grant of $10,000 towards the purchase of the land. It is estimated that the road will cost $20,000, which will be paid by the Provincial 'Government.
Where is the telescope being made?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Part of it is being made in Cleveland, and part in Pittsburgh.
What is the diameter?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Six feet. It is the largest in the world.

I do not wish to press the matter unduly or to ask for technical explanations that I would not understand even if the minister could make them, but again I say there must be some important purpose to be served by the installation of such a magnificent instrument as this, and I am sure the country would be interested in knowing just what the purpose is. We do not want this information for purposes of criticism, but simply to understand the object the astronomical department has in view.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand it is to enlarge the scope of the present work, which they claim is not at all commensurate with what should be done in a country like this. It would be no good for me to go into the technical details for I could not do it justice; but I understand it is to do the work on a much larger scale than our present equipment will permit.
Is it research work, educative work, or astronomical?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Astronomical work, stars and other things.
As the House meets at 11 in the morning and the committees at 10, and as it is now 11 o'clock and we have put through a number of items this evening, I think the House might rise.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: We do not want to object at all, but the Secretary of State would like to get some of his Civil Government Estimates through to-night. We could make some progress in the next few minutes, and then adjourn.

I do not wish to press it very much, but the only person on this side of the House who could criticise the civil government of the Department of the Secretary of State is the ex-secretary, who does not happen to be here. I do not think there would be any time lost if the minister would adjourn.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I will go on to-morrow.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Rogers the House adjourned at 11.10 p.m.
Saturday, March 27, 1915.
